When was the last time U.S. Congress overrode a president's veto?

The U.S. Constitution gives Congress the ability to override a president's veto with a supermajority (⅔) vote.

What are the recent, say, 10 times the U.S. Congress overrode a president's veto?
gold_answers:
You can find a current list on the US Senate website: Vetoes, 1789 to Present.

The current most-recent instance was the House's (Dec. 28, 2020) and Senate's (Jan. 1, 2021) override of Trump's veto of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (H.R.6395), just two days before the transfer of power would begin.

A President typically will not veto something that will pass by override, and informally some bills are said to pass with a "veto-proof" majority. For context in this instance, Republicans in congress agreed to wrap up this issue before the transfer of power to their political opponents, but Trump was apparently not so concerned. He gave a variety of vague reasons but we also know that during this time he had planned to preventing the transfer of power culminating in the January 6th insurrection a few days later, which may explain the party's different views on urgency.

query:
How do I track a bill that has been passed out of committee?

This is a general question about the U.S. House of Representatives, but for specifics I will use HR 1320 of the 119th U.S. Congress. This bill was introduced Feb 13, 2025 and referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce. It passed out of committee on July 23, 2025.

My question is, "Now what?" The standard answer is, "It goes to the full House for debate and a vote," but that answer is short on details for someone who's trying to keep track of a bill. This blog post, if accurate, has a few more details, most notably that the Speaker of the House will work with the House Rules Committee to place the bill on one of four calendars.

For instance, the Union Calendar seems to the most common calendar. That appears to be available at govinfo.gov as a file that gets updated into a new file each day. Browsing through the most up-to-date one (Nov 10, linked above), I don't see any reference to HR 1320. I can conclude that in the three and a half months between when HR 1320 was passed from committee to today, the Speaker and the Rules Committee have not placed it on the Union Calendar to be debated and voted on. That's all I seem to be able to determine, though.

Is there any way of knowing the status of this bill during this time? Is there any way of knowing when the Speaker and Rules Committee will place the bill on one of the calendars, and which calendar it will be? Do I have to download PDFs of all four calendars every day to check to see if the bill has been added to one?
gold_answers:
The "Actions" tab on the bill web page is normally enough to track a bill. In this case, there is a misunderstanding concerning the distinction between "Ordered to be Reported" and "Reported."

You wrote (edited):

[H.R.1320] passed out of committee on July 23, 2025.

The bill is still in the committee awaiting a report.

Note that the latest action for H.R.1320 was (emboldening added),

Latest Action: House - 07/23/2025 Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 19 - 16

But that is not enough to send the bill to the floor and get it placed on a calendar.

Ordering the Bill Reported

... The bill is actually reported (as opposed to the committee ordering it reported) when the bill and the accompanying written committee report are submitted to the Clerk when the House is in session. ... [CRS]

The bill, once the report is available, will be placed on a calendar.

The distinction between "Reported" and "Ordered to be Reported" may be seen by this example from the actions on H.R.5349. Note the reference to the report for "Reported."

10/03/2025 Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 287.

10/03/2025 Reported (Amended) by the Committee on Ways and Means. H. Rept. 119-335.

09/17/2025 Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 40 - 0.

query:
Do any movements for the restoration of jus soli exist in countries that have eliminated it?

Per Wikipedia's article on jus soli (meaning 'right of soil', the right of anyone born in the territory of a state to nationality or citizenship):

Since the early 1980s (with the British Nationality Act 1981), developed countries have been restricting the right of jus soli (and jus sanguinis, as it happened to the Italian nationality law) in response to anti-immigration political pressures and to discourage economic migration from former colonies and non-developed countries.

Before the aforementioned changes, a fair number of countries, particularly in Europe, had jus soli regimes similar to those that continue to predominate in the Americas. Given that many of these changes occurred within approximately the last 40 years, and seemingly largely under conservative governments, one might imagine that there might still be some controversy around them, at least in some political groups.

Are there any political movements in these countries, particularly any major political parties, that advocate for the restoration of the previous status quo on jus soli?

Note: While the primary focus of my question is the countries that have eliminated jus soli since 1981, in particular those that are majority-ethnically European and might have been following the lead of the UK, any examples of countries with movements for the restoration of birthright citizenship are valid answers.
gold_answers:
For example the European Network on Statelessness ("a civil society alliance of organisations and individuals working to promote the right to a nationality in Europe.") promotes jus soli as way of avoiding statelessness. A discursive blog on their website concludes:

... Jus soli is an effective way to confer nationality in an inclusive manner and to strengthen prevention measures against statelessness at birth. Introducing jus soli-related provisions and safeguards also reflects the way in which European societies have changed in recent decades, and the important role immigration now plays in many countries of the continent. In this respect, Europe can learn a lot from the experiences of the Americas.

query:
What government policies have contributed to India's rise as a major geopolitical and economic power in the 21st century

In recent decades, India has increasingly been described as an emerging global power, both economically and politically. It is now one of the world's largest economies by GDP (PPP), has a growing military, and plays a significant role in international diplomacy (e.g., BRICS, G20, QUAD).

What domestic or foreign policy decisions by the Indian government have been most influential in this transformation? Are there specific reforms, strategies, or events since the 1990s that contributed significantly to India’s global positioning?
gold_answers:
(The hypothesis below comes from a Western, pro-free market, PoV).

Given the size and potential of its population and resources India should be further ahead than it is now, compared to its regional and historical peers. That the situation is improving is mostly due to jettisoning some romantic, but impractical, policies that it embarked on after independence and engaging in reforms and economic liberalization as a result of a crisis in 1991. Those reforms were initiated by PM NV Rao, of the Indian National Congress.

PM N. Modi, for all his well-publicized drift towards ethnic intolerance and identity politics, has been a "cautious reformer" as well (it's easy to find coverage either lauding or lambasting his achievements in that regard). So, perhaps a mixed record, but by comparison to some of his predecessors, at least not a disastrous one.

Technologically, with better telecoms and large proportions of English-speakers, India was also well-positioned to benefit from the shift to outsourcing and remote work.

Problems remain, including low women workforce participation rates 31% vs 54% elsewhere and a rather low adult literacy rate of 75% in 2018 as well as restrictive labor laws in a country with a large informal economic sector.

Under Nehru India entered the second half of the 20th century after its independence with a mixed baggage of attitudes towards the economy and capitalism, and a certain degree of liking for economic dirigisme and communist-style planning. Those attitudes may have been rooted in repulsion about how Indians were treated under the British rule, but that did not make them any more effective in practice.

For example, India ran 5 year plans from 1951 to 2017

A good deal of India's growth, starting from the early 1990s was due to jettisoning some of the dafter ideas their governments initially followed.

Will a harsher world accelerate India’s reforms? The Economist, August 2025

It would not be the first time. In recent weeks there has been chatter about “another 1991 moment”. That was the year when a balance-of-payments crisis triggered a wave of liberalisation, in which capital controls were lifted, and the dismantling of the “licence raj” began. In part, the comparison reveals how far India has already come. In 1991 the country was left on the verge of bankruptcy; with no money to buy oil, its economy ground to a halt. Almost half the population was living in extreme poverty; today it is less than one in 20. And India will soon be the world’s fourth-largest economy.

License Raj

The Licence Raj or Permit Raj (rāj, meaning "rule" in Hindi)1 is a term coined by Indian independence activist and statesman C. Rajagopalachari for the system of strict government control and regulation of the Indian economy. This economic system, a form of state capitalism, was in place from the 1950s to the early 1990s. Under this system, businesses in India were required to obtain licences from the government in order to operate, and these licences were often difficult to obtain.24

The Licence Raj was intended to protect Indian industry, promote self-reliance and ensure regional equality.6 Up to 80 government agencies had to be satisfied before private companies could produce something and, if granted, the government would regulate production.6

1991 Indian economic crisis - Wikipedia

One of the main causes of the crisis was the accumulation of foreign debt. In the 1980s, India had borrowed heavily from international lenders, in part to finance infrastructure projects and industrialisation. However, by 1991, the country was facing a severe balance of payments crisis, as it was unable to service its debt and was running out of foreign exchange reserves.[19] There were also structural problems in the Indian economy that contributed to the crisis, including low savings and investment rates, and inadequate export growth.

The foreign exchange reserves by 1991 had dried up to the point that India could barely finance three weeks worth of imports.

The reforms formally began on 1 July 1991 when RBI devalued the rupee by 9% and by a further 11% on 3 July. It was done in two doses to test the reaction of the market first by making a smaller depreciation of 9%.[33] The economic reforms pushed by Prime Minister Rao were met with significant opposition from those who believed that they resulted in a reduction of India's autonomy. The speech made by then Prime Minister Rao, a week after taking office, emphasized the need for these reforms. As reported by the New York Times, "Mr. Rao, who was sworn in as Prime Minister last week, has already sent a signal to the nation—as well as the I.M.F.—that India faced no "soft options" and must open the door to foreign investment, reduce the bureaucratic red tape that stifles initiative, and streamline industrial policy."[34]

book review re. Nehru

The affinity of Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister of independent India, for socialism is well documented and widely recognised. He openly identified as a socialist during the Lahore session of the Congress in 1929, significantly influenced by the Soviet model of planning, which advocated for a greater role of the state in economic affairs.

Nehru's writings and speeches from 1946 onwards reflect a notable transition from radical socialism to a more moderate form known as Fabian socialism. Despite this shift towards moderation, the underlying belief that wealth generation was inherently sinful persisted.

The introduction of the licence-quota permit system and the resulting autarky, along with the decision to invest capital in heavy industries despite a lack of labour, were deemed by Panagariya as the most inefficient use of both capital and labour resources.

autarkic tendencies

India remained a virtually closed economy for nearly four decades after its independence in 1947, following an inward-looking development strategy. The key goal was to achieve self-reliance in all possible dimensions of economic activities of the nation. The immediate aspiration of independent India was perhaps to mimic the development trajectories of the “advanced” industrialized nations, albeit very much within the framework of import substitution and self-reliance.

Weird taxation

Some of these things were truly bizarre. Working in the IT industry on multinational ERP systems, my coworkers and I were rather non-plussed at some of the taxation systems prevalent in India. query:
Poland invokes Article 4 of NATO Charter in response to Russian incursion, when and why has this Article been invoked before?

Poland invokes Article 4 of NATO’s charter, under which alliance members can demand consultations with their allies. Only the eighth time that article has been invoked since 1949. Poland does this in response to 19 Russian Drones crossing into their territory.

Question: What were the other 7 times Article 4 has been invoked?

Poland says it shot down Russian drones that violated its airspace during attack on Ukraine

“This situation brings us the closest we have been to open conflict since World War II," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.

Tusk said he had activated Article 4 of NATO’s treaty, under which alliance members can demand consultations with their allies, and that he was in touch with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, who called the incursion "reckless behavior," irrespective of whether it was deliberate.

A NATO official confirmed to NBC News that Poland had "requested consultations under Article 4 of the Washington Treaty,” only the eighth time that the article — which does not trigger a military reaction — has been invoked since NATO was established in 1949.
gold_answers:
Short answer

All 8 invocations have taken place since 2003. 5 times by Turkey, once regarding the Iraq war, once after the Suruç bombing, 3 times involving Syria. Twice by Poland, in 2014 and 2025, in response to actions by Russia. Once by multiple Eastern European members in 2022, in response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Complete list (excluding Poland in 2025):

Since the Alliance’s creation in 1949, Article 4 has been invoked seven times:

  1. On 10 February 2003, Türkiye formally invoked Article 4, asking for consultations in the NAC on defensive assistance from NATO in the event of a threat to its population or territory resulting from armed conflict in neighbouring Iraq. NATO agreed a package of defensive measures and conducted Operation Display Deterrence from the end of February to early May 2003.

  2. On 22 June 2012, Türkiye requested a NAC meeting under Article 4 after one of its fighter jets was shot down by Syrian air defence forces.

  3. On 3 October 2012, Türkiye requested Article 4 NAC consultations when five Turkish civilians were killed by Syrian shells. Following these incidents, on 21 November 2012, Türkiye requested the deployment of Patriot missiles. NATO agreed to this defensive measure to help Türkiye defend its population and territory, and to help de-escalate the crisis along the border.

  4. On 3 March 2014, Poland invoked Article 4 following increasing tensions in neighbouring Ukraine, as a result of Russia’s aggressive actions.

  5. On 26 July 2015, Türkiye requested that the NAC convene in view of the seriousness of the situation following terrorist attacks, and to inform Allies of the measures it was taking.

  6. On 28 February 2020, Türkiye requested consultations following the death of Turkish soldiers in air strikes by the Syrian regime and its backer Russia in Idlib province.

  7. On 24 February 2022, Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania and Slovakia requested to hold consultations under Article 4 following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

query:
Which US presidents were subpoenaed by Congressional committees?

In a recent article published by the BBC, Clintons subpoenaed to testify in congressional Epstein investigation, it is stated that five U.S. presidents have received subpoenas from Congressional committees:

Over the last 200 years, only four other former presidents have received subpoenas from congressional committees, and only two provided testimony.

Trump is included as one of those four presidents although the subpoena was dropped when the committee disbanded. The article is referring to Bill Clinton as "other former presidents". This implies that three additional former presidents received subpoenas by Congress. Who were they, and which of them provided testimony?
gold_answers:
Republican James Comer, chairman of the House Oversight Committee, issued the subpoenas to the Clintons and eight other individuals. [...]

Over the last 200 years, only four other former presidents have received subpoenas from congressional committees, and only two provided testimony.

WaPo (2022) includes this event as relevant:

In 1846, the House began investigating a former secretary of state, Daniel Webster, who had served under presidents John Tyler and John Quincy Adams, for misuse of funds. The sitting president, James K. Polk, gave a limited amount of information about the funds to the House but didn’t think it would be proper to “publicly reveal confidences of his predecessors,” according to Rotunda.

Congress convened two select committees and subpoenaed both former presidents. Tyler complied, testifying before both committees, and Adams filed a deposition. James Buchanan, a future president who was secretary of state at the time, was also subpoenaed and testified. Webster was cleared of wrongdoing.

So both Tyler and Adams were subpoenaed, and Adams partly cooperated. While Truman did not

In 1953, former president Harry S. Truman refused to comply with a House subpoena after he was accused of knowingly appointing a Russian spy to a position while in office. The House Un-American Activities Committee, vociferously engaged in interrogating anyone and everyone for alleged communism, subpoenaed Truman. He refused to comply, instead giving a national broadcast denying the accusation. The House didn’t push the matter.

And Trump too

Lincoln apparently testified voluntarily, but other presidents and ex-presidents have received subpoenas compelling them to testify before Congress, in civil and criminal proceedings, and even before a military tribunal. Former president Donald Trump joined this group Thursday when the House Jan. 6 committee voted unanimously to subpoena him.

Although WaPo has a somewhat confusing para about Nixon, saying he invoked Truman as precedent, Nixon was not actually subpoenaed by Congress to testify in person, but subpoenaed by them for tapes and some similar materials. Nixon was ordered by a court to testify in the trial of his adviser Ehrlichman. I haven't followed up on that, but I think ultimately Nixon didn't testify. The judge's order well entertained the possibility that Nixon would assert executive privilege. On the other hand, Reagan gave a videotaped deposition in the trial of Poindexter in the Contras affair. But that was not before Congress.

Also there's probably some confusion regarding Jefferson (in the other answer). He was seemingly not subpoenaed by Congress.

Other presidents, including Thomas Jefferson, James Monroe and Bill Clinton, have been subpoenaed — not before Congress but in civil, criminal and military proceedings.

Jefferson was subpoenaed to provide documents and to testify in the treason trial of his former vice president, Aaron Burr. He produced some of the requested documents but refused to testify, saying he was too busy as president to comply. (This move was upheld by the Supreme Court, giving rise to the concept of “executive privilege.”)

Jefferson was subpoenaed by the Chief Justice Marshall to produce some documents, not by Congress, and not to testify in person. Also the context of this was Burr's trial in 1807, more than 200 years before the BBC piece, so they're probably not counting that affair in their statement on that angle anyway.

A few others then-former presidents appeared similarly to Lincoln, without being formally subpoenaed

Other than Lincoln, a couple of presidents have volunteered to appear before Congress, Rotunda noted. Ford appeared before a House committee looking into his pardon of Nixon, and Theodore Roosevelt testified before congressional committees twice after leaving office, providing details about a questionable U.S. Steel deal and about corporate donations to his 1902 presidential campaign.

So my guess is that the BBC means Tyler, Adams, Truman and Trump were the "other" subpoenaed ones (besides Clinton) given the context they give. I'm less sure who are the two the BBC says provided testimony. Tyler for sure, and perhaps they count Adams' written deposition too.

If you want to take the BBC statement's with less context, then subpoenas for materials would apply too, and the list of such subpoenas is surely longer, including those for Nixon and G. W. Bush, who was so subpoenaed several times by Congress for materials.

query:
Why do Austrian political parties have so many members?

Browsing through List of largest political parties, I noticed that the ÖVP in Austria has 600,000 members (2017), or 6.8% of the population. This is much more than any party in other European democracies. For comparison, the next largest party in the EU is the Romanian PSD (509,000 or 2.55%), the Italian Democratic Party (412,675 or 0.69%), French Renaissance (411,892 or 0.64%), or German CDU (371,986 or 0.44%; the sister party CSU had just over 1% in Bavaria in 2019). The only other parties I could find with over 2% are Austrian SPÖ, with 180.000 members, 2.04% of the population, Croatian CDU (220,000 or 5.3%), and Romanian PSD (already mentioned). In most (medium to large) EU countries, parties with more than 0.5% of the population in members are rare (NB: the list only includes parties with more than 100.000 members, so small countries with high percentages are not covered).

Is there something special in Austria, or why are their party memberships an order of magnitude higher than in Germany? I think party membership used to be much higher in other countries (Dutch CDA dropped from more than 500.000 in the 1950s to 26.000 in 2025), so another way to phrase the question is how Austria has avoided the large drop in membership numbers that other countries have.
gold_answers:
Yes, indeed there is something special about Austria. There used to be a system called Proporz for distributing all kinds of positions in state-owned companies to members of the political parties (SPÖ and ÖVP, back then). So up to the 1990ies it was mostly required to be a member of a party for any kind of leadership position, but it did 'help' even for regular employee positions. The state-owned sector was also quite large - most of education, healthcare, communication, postal services, public transport and energy (from extraction/production to distribution) used to be state-owned.

The system is officially no longer used, but there is a lot of inertia. Plus a strong tradition of all kinds of clubs, from sports to motorists and even rescue organisations being affiliated to political parties.

query:
How frequently is foreign press barred or allowed in war zones?

(Yes, this is motivated by the question about press access to Gaza, but don't read support, or criticism, for that question in this one. Merely curiosity about how much we can expect free press access in conflict zones).

To give some context of my understanding coming into this question:

  • During the Vietnam War, the US, consciously or not, experimented with press freedom in a war zone. This was largely seen to have been a mistake from the US PoV, whether or not one agreed with war itself. From burning napalm on a child, to a self-immolating monk, to a spot execution of a bound communist sympathizer, a number of instantly-recognizable photos contributed in driving down US domestic support for the war.

I kinda recall people stating that that access had been a) unusual and b) mismanaged. With the unusual aspect relevant to my question here.

  • By Gulf War 1, the US had learned its lesson and the press coverage about press coverage was fascinated by the solution found: embedded journalists. Who were vetted, and controlled by, the Pentagon. So, yes, there was access. But, no, it wasn't free access. And, if I recall correctly, no one was much surprised or outraged, just a bit cynical about the press freedom quotient to be expected.

  • In the Ukraine war, the press does have access to the Ukraine side of things. But even people highly sympathetic to Ukraine can understand that Ukraine has a vested interest in presenting its plight on the world stage. Free press access is of benefit to Ukraine, which is not doubt a huge part of the reasons it is allowed.

    • On the Russian side of things, no, I don't think there is free access to foreign journalists to the occupied regions. They do conduct tours, of sorts, mostly with picked Western "journalists" of dubious quality.

  • India has found it expedient at times to bar foreign press in Kashmir for months at a time. RSF in 2020: "The Kashmir Valley, from which foreign reporters had already been barred for several months"

  • Yes, there are plenty of counterinsurgency conflicts - presumably what Gaza is supposed to be at this point - where press is allowed, under various levels of control, by the official government. But in many cases, the "coverage of the coverage" also points out the reason: the government wants to appear strong and in control and a press blackout would give the opposite impression. Keep that in mind when looking at historical access to Gaza - just because it was allowed at one time doesn't mean the same calculation about the cost/benefit applies nowadays, from the Israeli side.

    • Yes, at times Israel has allowed foreign press into Gaza, under highly controlled conditions, for example to show tunnels under hospitals. This is akin to Gulf War 1 embedded reporters and isn't generally seen as free press access.

  • Guerrillas, rebels and sometimes even terrorists often explicitly covet coverage, consider press access a tool in their struggle and therefore allow it. But, like Ukraine, one should be under no illusion about why this is allowed, regardless of where one's sympathy lies.

So, on balance is foreign press access the norm, or the exception, in conflict zones, on the government side? Especially by democracies, rather than authoritarian regimes.

p.s. At the risk of stating the obvious, the press itself will almost always insist on press freedom. This question isn't about what the press thinks, nor whether public opinion thinks that the press should be allowed or not. It is concerned with what is normative/customary with regards to foreign press access in war zones.

p.p.s. Be cautious about survivor bias here. Merely citing all the conflict coverage you can recall doesn't tell us much about the cases where it wasn't allowed.

p.p.p.s. It was already in the comments, but it seems to have been missed: while it is motivated by the Gaza situation this question is explicitly not about Gaza: we already know the foreign press is barred there.
gold_answers:
I rather doubt you'll find a comprehensive survey on this that objectively manages to quantify the level of access. But to quote the nutshell from 2000 one:

States frequently expect high degree of compliance from their media in wartime, usually rationalised on grounds of operational security and the protection of militarily sensitive information demanded by the war effort.

[...] The British correspondent Max Hastings during the Falklands conflict famously remarked, "When one's nation is at war, reporting becomes an extension of the war effort. Objectivity only comes back into fashion when the black-out comes down".

And yes, that paper agrees with you that the level of access that (US) journalists had during the Vietnam war was exceptional (and thus unusual both relative to precedents and to what came after), although that certainly didn't apply to connex theatres like Laos.

The military in the first world was learning that you should handle the press by denying access and then acquiesce when they were ready to do a deal. Thereafter the approach has been used in Grenada, Panama and during the Gulf War.

[...] The media management at Kosovo outdid that [Vietnam] record: he calls it the most refined model for journalistic death. There were 2700 people from the media accompanying the NATO forces when they entered the province at the end of the bombing campaign. There were daily briefings, military meetings, press conferences and endless arranged interviews all of which did not add up to news, but the journalists were kept too busy to notice. Much later, the stories they had missed, began to sink in.

You'd be hard pressed to find a more comprehensive survey that you've already provided in your Q.

You will find much longer discussions about objectivity (or lack thereof) from war zone correspondents.

And if you'd rather read an equally long narrative about the press-military relations through the ages (but again rather focused on the US) there is one other chapter in the same book dealing with that. But you'd be hard pressed to find objective metrics of access used, and that chapter too often delves more into the issue of objectivity in reporting. And in lieu of any (more) statistics it has this (perhaps interesting) vignette as its conclusion section

Pilger reveals that out of 649 journalists accredited to the Saigon press corps from 1968, only about eight of them made regular forays into the field (2001, p. 263). Jacques Leslie remembers it differently. He says that ‘most journalists, unless they were too frightened or concerned for their safety, got out of Saigon – the good stories weren’t in Saigon’. He takes credit for being the first American correspondent to go into Viet Cong territory, ‘only because of the arrival of the ceasefire in late January, 1973. Before that, it was impossible – anyone trying before that was likely to enjoy the fate of my friend Alex Shimkin, a Newsweek stringer, who blundered into Viet Cong territory in 1972 and was immediately killed.’ He does not see his actions as particularly daring or heroic. It was about being sensible and about being a good journalist. He had simply nurtured good contacts and sources, in this case Viet Cong sources, who assured him that with the ceasefire in place he would be safe and that he would be treated well. As he points out, ‘it wasn’t laziness on the part of other journalists that kept them out – rather, it was a quite reasonable fear of being killed, and the dearth of sources like mine.’ Once he set the example and showed it could be done, others followed his footsteps, some of them quite literally ‘to the very village I’d visited, until the village chief told them they were taking up too much of his time, and to pass the word to stop going there.’ The majority of journalists never considered meeting the Viet Cong because they had nothing to learn. The VC were the enemy, they were evil; end of story. Leslie’s bureau chief, George McArthur, ‘rarely left Saigon for any reason, relied on his CIA sources for many if not most of his stories, and probably figured anyone who pulled off the feat would be treated to nothing more than a Potemkin Village-like performance for his efforts.’

As for more recent conflicts... take this account

I have a unique view of the war in Afghanistan, having spent much more time among Afghans than Americans. I arrived in 2012 to report for Reuters, when the US presence was winding down. I left after serving as the Wall Street Journal’s bureau chief in Kabul in late 2017, and continued to follow the war from Washington, DC, where I cover foreign policy for the paper.

The US military refused to offer meaningful access in those years, so I often embedded with Afghan forces instead, or traveled alone with Afghan reporters, under the cover of a burqa where necessary.

[...] Throughout this period, the Pentagon granted virtually no media access to US operations, and the increasing reliance on special operations forces happened out of public view. In the absence of a reality check, the rules of engagement remained designed for the fictional training mission the administration wanted, rather than what was actually happening.

To be sure, the Pentagon’s resistance to allowing journalists access to complex and risky operational environments is understandable. And the media shares some of the blame: every major US television network pulled out of Afghanistan after most US troops left, and only a few newspapers were willing to continue the investment as reporting became more difficult.

One of the problems for journalists trying to embed with Afghan forces in far-flung places was getting there in the first place. The US military often flew troops and supplies to these locations and could plausibly have taken journalists too (as it did in Vietnam, for example). But this never happened. Instead, when we embedded with Afghan forces in Kunar, or Nangarhar, or Kunduz, we drove to them in our unarmored Toyota Corollas at great personal risk. We made these trips as often as we could convince our editors it was worthwhile, but the lack of cooperation from the military hindered access for us and other media outlets. It apparently originated from meetings of finance ministers of first 4 countries that met semi regularly and when in 1974 there were changes of government due to scandals and whatnot, in France, West Germany, Italy, Japan, UK and US and because they faced global international problems about which they wanted to discuss, these group of inexperienced heads of government met for a retreat in 1975 to discuss their course of action in an informal meeting and decided to make that a yearly thing. How do the 2023-2024 university pro-Gaza protests compare to other political protests in the US in terms of violence/illegal acts?

Short Answer

The 2023-2024 university pro-Gaza protests were not particularly exceptional the terms of violence or illegal acts in recent U.S. history.

There are many examples of more violent protest movements in recent U.S. history, and many more of comparable violent/illegal acts by protest movements in recent U.S. history. These protests are even more mild when compared to violent protests in the longer sweep of U.S. history.

The facts do not support the assertion that pro-Gaza protests at U.S. colleges and universities have been particularly violent or particularly exceptional compared to other modern protest movements in resorting to illegal activity.

Most of the violent riots and instances of civil unrest in the last 45 years have involved unpremeditated grass roots responses to incidents of alleged police misconduct, or spontaneous reactions to the outcomes of major sporting events. Violence and major illegal activity surrounding planned political protests, in general, and in the case of the pro-Gaza protests in the U.S. in particular, has been much more modest in the vast majority of cases.

The amount of "street politics" utilized in the U.S. is lower than that of most countries in Europe, Latin America, and much of the rest of the world, and has been comparatively scarce since the 1980s compared to historical levels.

Long Answer

The Baseline

The pro-Gaza protests at colleges and universities in the U.S. since October 7, 2023, is part of a larger, multinational protest movement that has used different tactics at different times, in different places.

Mostly, the illegal acts at the pro-Gaza protests at U.S. colleges and universities within this movement, have involved trespassing, failure to disperse at the direction of law enforcement, and relatively minor property damage and littering, although there have been one or two incidents giving rise to minor personal injuries for law enforcement or security officials, whom protestors do not appear to have set out to harm at the outset. The vast majority of pro-Gaza protests (an estimated 97%) have been completely non-violent. There have been more incidents of intentional violence directed at pro-Gaza protestors by pro-Israel counterprotestors (which were serious in at least a couple of cases), even though those incidents have been much less common, than there have been by the primary pro-Gaza protestors.

Marches in Washington D.C. for the pro-Gaza cause have been neither particularly large, compared to many other Washington D.C. protest Marches in recent times, nor particularly small, and have not been violent.

Examples Of More Violent Or Illegal Protests In U.S. History

These examples are a convenience sample and are not intended to be comprehensive or to constitute a valid random sample for statistical purposes. But, it is a sufficient sample to answer the question and includes many of the most notable incidents in post-WWII U.S. history, as well as a handful of cases from the pre-WWII era.

This list of examples under samples the voluminous list of violent political protests during the tumultuous period in U.S. history of the 1960s and early 1970s, and also under samples the catalog of violent incidents related to labor union activism from the late 1940s to the early 1960s, when strikes and other labor actions were profoundly more common in the U.S.

For the most part, the comparison of these incidents to the pro-Gaza protests in this answer are qualitative, rather than specifying a quantitative level of harm caused. In particular, the core factor singling these incidents as worse than the pro-Gaza protests or not, in terms of violence and illegality, has been the extent to which the protests caused injuries or deaths, and the extent to which the protests caused property damage, such as burning vehicles or buildings or destroying infrastructure, that involved more than the incidental or minor property damage, which is inevitable in any large gathering of people.

Arrests for trespassing, public order offenses, and littering, which are ubiquitous even at a large swath of protests of all kinds and are often dismissed before going to trial, have been disregarded. Likewise, the level of disruption caused by non-violent protests has been largely dismissed as a relevant factor, as it is also ubiquitous in all forms of non-violent protest activity, and is often not illegal.

The examples of protests more violent or with qualitatively more illegality than the pro-Gaza protests at colleges and universities in the U.S. is as follows:

Protest Movements Comparable To the Gaza Protests

There are many cases in U.S. history of activism that was pretty comparable to that of the Gaza protestors in terms of the illegality of their tactics. For example:

The widely shared norm, among even hard-core activists in the U.S., that protests should be non-violent, is often attributed to Martin Luther King, Jr.'s leadership during the U.S. Civil Rights movement in the 1950s and 1960s, and he explicitly attributed the firm adoption of this strategy to the efforts of Gandhi in India's movement for independence from Britain.

A list of notable incidents of civil unrest in the United States, shows that only some of them were political.

Riots and the 2009 San Francisco riots in reaction to the killing of Oscar Grant by a law enforcement officer), not all of which were violent. Context: The Trump Administration's characterization of the protests

The characterization of the pro-Gaza protests as "anti-semitic" in the sense of being anti-Jewish (a claim that the Trump Administration has frequently made), is also generally not well founded.

Few American Jews take the position that the October 7, 2023 act was justified, although some recognize that they can understand what helped motivate it. Generally, American Jews see this Hamas attack as a horrible tragedy. But many American Jews also feel that the Israeli government has not shown sufficient regard for the human rights of the people in Gaza and that the Israeli government has responded in a disproportionate manner to the attacks. Caveats

This answer also does not address notable cases of violent responses to protests such as the Kent State Shootings in 1970, the MOVE bombing by the Philadelphia police in 1985, and many violent union busting actions directed at labor activists in U.S. labor history (especially by the Pinkerton Detective Agency).

Footnote on labor activism in the U.S.

Wikipedia notes six general strikes in U.S. history, one in 1919 in Seattle, and four in 1934, at the height of the Great Depression, one in Toledo, one in Minneapolis, one in San Francisco and one at West Coast Ports. There was also a general strike in the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico in 1998. The last general strike in the English Speaking United States was 76 years ago, and very few people living today remember it. The United States has never had a nationwide general strike and just two general strikes in its history, one restricted to a single industry, and the other to a U.S. territory, that extended beyond a single city.

Union-management relations in the United States used to look a lot like they do in Europe. Strikes were large, frequent and involved a large share of the work force. National guard forces or private security forces were frequently called in to put them down in bloody conflicts. Openly socialist political parties were organized.

In 1950, a year that revisionist history remembers as a tranquil period in American history, there were 424 strikes involving 1,000 or more workers, in all involving 1,698,000 workers, which was more than one in nine members of the unionized workforce of 14.3 million workers who made up 31.5% of the total work force.

In 2008, there were 15 strikes involving 1,000 or more workers, in all including 72,000 workers which was one in two-hundred and twenty-three members of the unionized workforce of 16.1 million workers who made up 12.4% of the total workforce. The public sector which is 36.8% unionized, is as unionized as the private sector was at its peak. The private sector, which is 7.2% unionized, has the lowest level of unionization in the private sector since the 1920s, if not earlier.

The unionized workforce has remained more or less constant for half a century, despite a growing workforce, and that masks the fact that there has been substantial growth in public sector union membership and a substantial decline in private sector union membership over that time period.

In the United States, there has been only one year since 1983 that more than 3% of unionized workers went on strike (1986), and there has only been one year since 1998 (the year 2000) when more than one in eighty union members went on strike. In the entire United States from 1990 to 2008, there wasn't a single year that there were more than 45 strikes involving 1,000 or more workers in the entire United States, in a period that started with a labor force of 103 million workers and peaked at just short of 130 million workers. In contrast, there wasn't a single year from 1950 to 1987 that had less than 46 strikes, despite that fact that the workforce was significantly smaller. Prior to the 1980s there were a couple hundred major strikes in the United States per year, about ten times current levels of labor action.

Almost all strikes in recent memory have involved workers at just a single employer. Those strikes that do happen have mostly been pretty tame by international standards. American labor unions do not, as the French do, for example, kidnap members of management until a deal is reached.

Japan is probably the only other developed country in the world with a lower level of recent labor action.

An international perspective

Europe and many other nations of the world have far more political violence than the U.S.

For example, consider November and December of the year 2010, in Europe. In Spain, members of rival political parties beat each other up as demonstrators and counter-demonstrators clashed, controversial arrests led to street protests, and informal labor actions put Spanish air traffic controllers under martial law supervision; Portugal had a widely successful general strike; Greece was experiencing general strikes and violent clashes between demonstrators and law enforcement; controversial parliamentary votes in Italy triggered riots in Rome; the streets of Dublin were full of Irish citizens protesting austerity plans; and even London had tens of thousands of demonstrators doing things like walking over police cars and breaking the windows of Prince Charles' car while he was in it.

Major strikes, general strikes, street demonstrations, violent clashes between demonstrators and police, and all sorts of "street politics" outside formal political channels are far more common in most European political systems and labor relations than they are in the U.S. If you looked back just a little further, you'd find similar activity in France and many other European countries. Spain, France and Italy have all had general strikes since the 1980s. Spain and Northern Ireland have had on and off armed insurgencies in my lifetime. Greece and Germany have both had domestic terrorism in that time period.

Latin America, South Korea, and much of the rest of the world, has followed this pattern of politics that spill outside the constitutional process into the streets, and of labor relations that produce frequent labor actions as strategic tools in negotiations between labor and management.

There are occasional large marches and public demonstrations in the United States, and even some small scale clashes between police and demonstrators. But, the United States has really seen nothing like what Europe and much of the rest of the world experiences on a regular basis in terms of street politics in the last thirty years. Even the turbulent activism and political violence of the 1960s and 1970s in the United States was probably not quite as intense as what much of Europe has experienced in the last twenty or thirty years.

Less-developed countries have frequently seen their politics erupt into civil wars, or as in the cases of Haiti and Somalia, sometimes outright anarchy.

Political violence has been comparatively very rare in the U.S., and mass demonstration have been mostly both rare and mostly peaceful.

It isn't that the U.S. has had particularly low levels of violence generally. Its murder rate was the highest in the developed world for much of this time period. Crime rates in the U.S. are quite low by historical standards at the moment, but the lack of political violence in the United States in the last thirty years hasn't been strongly linked to overall violent crime rates.

query:
To what extent did the U.S. arms embargo during the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War influence India’s military and diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union?

Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has claimed that this embargo "pushed" India toward Russia, implying a significant shift in India’s foreign policy and military reliance (YouTube link) when historical context suggests India’s ties with the Soviet Union were already developing before 1965.

India, under Jawaharlal Nehru, pursued a policy of non-alignment after gaining independence in 1947, maintaining relations with both Western and Eastern blocs. By the 1950s, the U.S. had forged military alliances with Pakistan through SEATO and CENTO, providing Pakistan with significant arms support. Meanwhile, India’s relations with the Soviet Union had been warming, notably with Soviet backing during the 1962 Sino-Indian War. In 1965, during the Indo-Pakistani War over Kashmir, the U.S. imposed an arms embargo on both India and Pakistan.

In 1965, India's military inventory included British (Centurion tanks, Hawker Hunters), French (AMX-13 tanks), and increasingly Soviet (MiG-21s, T-54s) equipment. Battle accounts from 1965—such as the Battle of Asal Uttar or the air engagements—show India using these systems, with no significant mention of U.S.-origin weapons playing a decisive role.

To what extent did the U.S. arms embargo during the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War influence India’s military and diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union?
gold_answers:
To what extent did the U.S. arms embargo during the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War influence India’s military and diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union?

Only a little.

Soviet-India relations steadily warmed starting in the late 1950s and culminated in the 1971 Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation. The embargo had nearly nothing to do with this. Instead, by far the most important factor was their mutual hatred and fear of a common enemy: China.

Below, I give a sketch of the evolution of Soviet-India Relations.

The unimportance of the embargo is attested to by the fact that in a 41-page survey of Soviet-India relations from the 1950s through 1991, no mention is made of the embargo at all (Vojtech Mastny, "The Soviet Union’s Partnership with India", 2010).

You claim that

S. Jaishankar has claimed that this embargo "pushed" India toward Russia, implying a significant shift in India’s foreign policy

I watched the linked YouTube video and the above claim is a great exaggeration of what S. Jaishankar actually said. The discussion was solely on defense and arms:

Interviewer: Traditionally, for defense industry cooperation your main partner was Russia and that was a point of tension as I recall with the United States ...

S. Jaishankar: ... India was importing defense equipment from the United States till 1965. It was the United States which cut off India in 1965. It was the United States thereafter which did not resume sale of defense equipment to India from 1965 till 2006 barring one exception. ...

If India turned to Soviet Union and to thereafter to Russia, to a large extent it was a situation also created by the United States, which actually consciously had a policy of not supplying military equipment to India. So if they didn't want to sell it to us, ... that cannot then become a complaint against us. ...

Now it was not that we bought only from Russia in that same period. ... we bought planes from UK, we bought from France, we bought equipment from Germany, we bought from Israel.

The YouTube video title ("U.S. Cut Off India In 1965, That Pushed Us Towards Russia - So They Can't Complain!") was clickbait. Ignore it, listen carefully to the video, and you'll find that Jaishankar did not come close to making your much stronger claim that the embargo impl[ied] a significant shift in India’s foreign policy.

It is fair to say that solely in terms of arms imports, the US embargo pushed India more towards the USSR. But it also pushed India more towards other countries. And, to repeat and emphasize, the embargo did NOT impl[y] a significant shift in India’s foreign policy or heavily influence India's military and diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union.

Soviet-India Relations

(Unless otherwise stated, all citations and quotes from Mastny, 2010.)

Mid- to late-1950s

Stalin saw India as a "Western puppet" and Soviet-India relations "were limited". Ties grew warmer after Stalin's death in 1953. Circa 1955,

In pushing a strategy of “peaceful coexistence,” Khrushchev was trying to reverse recent Soviet setbacks in Europe by opening a “second front” of the Cold War in Asia. His rapprochement with India reflected that calculation. ...

Khrushchev and other intrinsically insecure Soviet leaders still needed "a major, high-profile, developing country like India [that would] be unabashedly friendly. It made a difference to their self-esteem and the perception of others."

India too

predicted that the Soviet Union would bring in factories, goods, development experience, technical expertise, and more ... foresaw political benefits ... at a time when the United States was "picking off one weak or compliant Asian State after another and hitching it to its wagon."

Nehru

saw both superpowers as sinful but believed that the Soviet Union was more capable of redemption because it was untainted by the evils of racism and colonialism.

In 1955, Nehru visited Moscow, where

the sight of Nehru had "a visible effect on the Soviet leaders. ... He came, saw, and conquered."

In 1956, India even refused to vote at the UN to condemn the USSR's suppression of the Hungarian uprising. (This was "fiercely criticized in the Indian press".)

Nonetheless, at this point,

The benefit Moscow derived from India's forbearance was largely symbolic ... India' benefit from Soviet friendship until then had been mainly economic and symbolic

In 1957, Zhukov visited India.

Late 1950s Onwards: China, the Common Enemy

The Sino-Soviet split is well-known: Ties badly soured in the late 1950s and early 1960s. In 1969, this would culminate in border clashes and the USSR contemplating a large-scale nuclear strike on China (arguably the closest the world has ever been to nuclear war).

What's perhaps less well-known is that Soviet support for India was one of the factors contributing to this split. And in turn, the split contributed to ever-warmer Soviet-India relations (in a positive feedback loop).

Prior to the late 1950s, India and China had initially been somewhat friendly members of the non-aligned fraternity: India found China a

congenial partner because of their common resentment of Western imperialism.

But in the late 1950s, relations began to sour:

  • In 1958, a conference on the border dispute failed.
  • In March 1959, with the Tibetan uprising, India gave asylum to the Dalai Lama (and also many Tibetan refugees), much to China's displeasure.
  • In August 1959, "a skirmish on the Sino-Indian border ... produced the first casualties".
  • In August 1959, the USSR extended India a $375 million line of credit (about $4.05B today).

The Chinese leaders claimed that the Soviet Union “deliberately took sides with India,” accusing it of “accommodation and compromise on important matters of principle.” The reference was to the divergence between Khrushchev's strategy of peaceful coexistence, which envisaged India as an ally in the competition with the West, and Mao's strategy of "international class struggle," which classified India as an enemy. The ideological dispute came to be intertwined with the border dispute as Mao escalated the struggle by engaging in personal attacks on Nehru, calling him "half-man, half-devil," among other epithets.

In October 1959, there was another deadly Sino-Indian border clash.

In July 1961, the US agreed to supply Pakistan with F-104s. In response, in May 1962, India made a deal with the USSR to buy MiGs and also set up MiG factories in India. (This raised serious concern in Washington and London.)

On 20 October 1962, following "probing actions" by India since June and relatively minor skirmishes, Mao decided to go to war with India: this was the brief Sino-Indian war (ended on 21 November). (Aside: Mao probably decided to do this at least in part because the two superpowers were preoccupied by the Cuban Missile Crisis, 16 to 28 October.)

Hasan (1968):

the event which had the most far-reaching impact on Soviet policy towards South Asia, especially Pakistan, was the Sino-Indian border conflict of October 1962.

China would detonate its first atom bomb in 1964 and its first hydrogen bomb in 1966, adding to the fears of both India and the USSR.

In May 1966, Mao launched the Cultural Revolution. What had previously already been fairly rabid ideological attacks on the USSR grew even stronger and more belligerent. And as already mentioned, in 1969, these attacks escalated to actual and dangerous border clashes and nuclear war was only narrowly avoided.

Altogether, by the mid- to late-1960s, India and the USSR had a very clear and common nuclear-armed enemy in China, which would ensure their ties continuously strengthened.

In August 1971, India and the USSR signed a Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation. Even this Treaty was pushed through by developments in China:

The Soviet-Indian pact was expedited once the Sino-American rapprochement provided a stimulus. Three weeks after the announcement of President Richard Nixon's forthcoming trip to Beijing, Soviet Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko rushed to Delhi to sign the pact on 7 August.

The 1965 Embargo

Perhaps surprisingly, the embargo was actually good for India. This is because the US (and UK) embargoed both India and Pakistan, and Pakistan was the weaker party. McGarr (The Cold War in South Asia, 2013, p. 326):

policymakers on both sides of the Atlantic calculated that Pakistan would suffer disproportionately from the imposition of a Western arms embargo, giving Ayub Khan [president of Pakistan] a powerful incentive to sue for peace. ... George Ball, US Under Secretary of State, noted that ‘Pakistan had [military] supplies only for three weeks, while India was in a much better position: in appearing to treat both sides equally, they [Britain and the US] had in fact treated them unequally’.

So, "[d]espite Indian protests to the contrary", India actually benefited from the embargo and were probably secretly pleased.

The subsequent failure of the US to resume military aid to India also benefited India for the same reason: The US also refused to resume military aid to Pakistan. Moreover, the US had been giving much more military aid to Pakistan than to India. CIA (1965):

Military aid delivered to India (starting in 1963) has amounted to $92 million and to Pakistan (starting in 1954) $676.7 million.

Hasan (1967):

It soon became obvious that India had no serious objections to the revised policy. Even immediately after the US announcement was made, traces of optimism could be detected beneath the surface of the resentment and anger which were expressed. It was generally acknowledged that while this major change in American policy would have a nominal effect on India, Pakistan would have to pay heavily for its dependence on the United States. The Times of India commenting on this development observed, "... This would mean ... the consolidation of the status quo in Kashmir by depriving Pakistan of the means by which it can artificially keep this issue alive." Gradually India adopted an attitude of complacency. ...

Pakistan ... protested to Washington that by placing Pakistan at par with India the United States was discriminating against the former, as Pakistan was more dependent on American arms than India was. ...

Its [Pakistan's] greater dependence on United States arms is proved by the following figures: since 1954, Pakistan has received $1,500 million worth of military aid from the US and till 1965 its armed forces were equipped entirely with American weapons, out of a total of $375 million worth of military assistance which India has received from the two big Powers, the United States has supplied $75 million. These figures indicate that at this stage the stoppage of American arms aid would have a marginal effect on India's war capacity, as its other major suppliers of arms are Britain and the Soviet Union. Britain, which had suspended the sales of arms to the subcontinent during September 1965, resumed deliveries in March 1966. ... Furthermore, Pakistan does not have much scope for indigenous production of arms. India, which started with a firmer footing than its neighbour, has an internal production capacity 25 times that of Pakistan. Besides small arms, it is even building factories for the manufacture of MIG aircraft. Hence the United States decision to discontinue arms aid will adversely affect Pakistan rather than India.

Also, Hasan (1968):

The Indian armed forces outnumber Pakistan by four to one.

Altogether, given all of the above and Pakistan's inherently weaker position (much smaller population, production, and armed forces; and severely weakened after the Bangladesh War of Independence, 1971), this apparently equal treatment of the US of India and Pakistan actually benefited India (at least vis-à-vis Pakistan).

It is correct to claim that the US embargo helped "push" India to buy more arms from elsewhere—but this merely included and was not limited to the USSR. To repeat what S. Jaishankar stated:

we bought planes from UK, we bought from France, we bought equipment from Germany, we bought from Israel.

Hasan (1967):

Within a year after the war of September 1965, India had also acquired 600 tanks from Eastern Europe.

But importantly, in that same year, India also acquired

over 400 heavy guns, 200 tanks transporters, a landing ship and 50 naval aircraft from West European Powers.

Summary: It is wrong to claim, as you do, that the embargo marked a "significant shift in India’s foreign policy", but OK to claim that it caused India to buy more arms from elsewhere (other than the US).

By the way, the caricature that from the 1960s, India turned mainly to the USSR, while Pakistan turned mainly to China is also much exaggerated. Hasan (1968) describes how from the 1962 Sino-Indian War, the USSR had turned from being solidly pro-India and anti-Pakistan to being a largely fair and neutral arbiter that happily sold arms to both (to India from 1962 and to Pakistan from 1968).

query:
Is there a precedent, in France, for barring a politician from running for office due to (political) fraud or embezzlement?

Shock Marine Le Pen verdict rocks French far right

"Incredible." That was the single word uttered under her breath by Marine Le Pen as she stormed out of a Paris courtroom on Monday morning.

She left the court early – just before hearing that she was barred from running for office for five years after being found guilty of embezzlement of EU funds – almost certainly ruling her out from standing in the 2027 French presidential election.

I knew she was in the dock for fraudulent use of EU funds. But even yesterday she seemed confident she'd not get barred from running. And the BBC article covering the subject seemed to find a possible prohibition not entirely normative.

Meantime, in the 80s and 90s, there were a number of scandals involving politicians, not least wrt Chirac. In the case of Chirac, whatever shady behavior happened ("fou de legumes" was a typical headline *), he wasn't accused of self-enrichment. And he did run for President. And in the case of LePen, she's accused of funding her own political staffers on the EU's dime.

Don't take this as any great sympathy for LePen. Only asking how past penalties to other prominent politicians compared: were they disqualified from running as well? And was that disqualification applied in the same manner?

* "crazy about veggies". Parts of the fraud, at Paris City Hall, consisted of over/duplicate invoicing for food and catering, so that the skimmed funds could go into the party's campaign coffers. So, at some point, him and his wife were eating like $200 of veggies per day between the 2 of them!
gold_answers:
The title of the BBC article is more sensational than accurate. The verdict wasn't shocking: it was pretty much anticipated. Given the facts that came out during the trial, it was likely that several of the accused, including Le Pen, would be found guilty. The loss of political rights (both voting and running for office) for a few years is one of the penalties for the offense that Le Pen was found guilty of (alongside fines and prison time).

This is not the first time a presidential hopeful is disqualified from running in an election due to being found guilty of embezzling public or private funds. There have been at least:

  • Bernard Tapie was a businessman who went into politics with a minor center-left party1. He might have run in the 1995 presidential election, but didn't, in part because he was under trial for corruption in sports. He was declared ineligible shortly after the presidential election.
  • Alain Juppé was a prominent right-wing politician, notably prime minister from 1995 to 1997. He was made ineligible for two years in 2004 for his role in embezzling funds of the Paris city council through a fake employee scheme. He was generally seen as a likely successor of the then president Jacques Chirac. The election wasn't until 2007, in which the candidate from Juppé's party was Nicolas Sarkozy, who won the election. If Juppé hadn't had to pause his involvement in politics, he would have been in a better position to win his party's nomination. He later ran in the same party's primary for the 2017 presidential election, where he lost to François Fillon.
  • François Fillon is a prominent right wing politician, notably prime minister from 2007 to 2012, and candidate in the 2017 presidential election. He ran (and came a close third) while indicted for embezzling private and public money, for which he was found eventually found guilty. He is currently ineligible. If not for his conviction, he might have been in the running for the 2022 presidential election.
  • Nicolas Sarkozy is a prominent right wing politician, notably president from 2007 to 2012. He lost a bid for reelection in 2012 and lost to François Fillon in his party's primary for the 2017 presidential election. He kept out of politics for a few years, but since 2022 he has been close to president Emmanuel Macron, and he was a potential candidate in the 2027 election, although with low chances given the high number of potential candidates at this stage. He was convicted in 2024 for bribing a judge and lost his civil rights for three years (expiring after the presidential election). He is also under trial for illegal campaign financing, for which a longer loss of civil rights is likely.
  • A near miss: François Bayrou is a prominent right-wing politician who ran for president in 2002, 2007 and 2012, and is now prime minister. He was accused of embezzling money from the European parliament in the same manner as Marine Le Pen (using EU money to pay people to work for the national party, even though that money is legally only allowed to be used for work that is directly related the European parliament), although to a much lesser scale. Some of the accused were found guilty and received a suspended sentence of ineligibility, but Bayrou himself was not found guilty (it is suspected that he participated, but the evidence is not sufficient to conclude).

The only difference I can think of between these cases and Le Pen's is that Le Pen has been her party's designated presidential candidate for over a decade, whereas the others had fierce internal competition so a replacement was found. This would be a strange basis to make an exception for Le Pen.

The court had a choice of whether or not to suspend Le Pen's civil rights. Under the law as it is now (“loi Sapin 2”), the offense carries an automatic penalty of loss of civil rights, but that only became law in 2016 a few months after Le Pen's offense ended. So according to the applicable law, the loss of civil rights was a possibility, alongside a fine and prison time. The judgment justifies the application of the penalty by the fact that the offence was especially egregious (basically, for a few years, this was a major part of balancing the party's budget), and that there is a serious risk of reoffending since many of the convicted persons are still active in politics and have expressed no remorse. To cite the judgment (my translation):

(…) the defence's arguments tended, notably even before any debate on the facts, to contest that criminal law could apply to the facts or to the persons who are under trial. (…) This defence system constitutes, in the eyes of the court, a theoretical construct that negates the rules of the European Parliament, the laws of the Republic and the legal verdicts established notably during the investigation for the present affair. (…)

Beyond a willingness to avoid or delay any debate around the facts that they were accused of, the defendants tried to withdraw from any substantial debate. Most of the defendants showed no willingness to participate in establishing the truth, with which some have a very distant connection, going so far as to deny the obvious, including what they themselves wrote at the time. (…)

Beyond the gravity of the offence which justifies ineligibility penalties for some of the defendants, we must be mindful that many defendants currently hold public offices or are planning to run for offices. There is thus a persisting risk that the individuals concerned may fraudulently dispose of public funds that they would be receiving, holding, allocating or using as part of such offices. This can only be prevented by declaring this conviction to be applicable provisionally2. (…)

The court takes into consideration, in addition to the risk of reoffending, the major trouble to democratic public order that would result in having as a candidate, for example and notably in the presidential election, and possibly even electing, a person who would have been convicted in the first jurisdiction to a sentence of ineligibility and whose conviction might be made definitive after the appeal.

The court must thus ensure that public office holders, like any person facing justice, do not benefit from a more favorable special treatment, which is incompatible with the trust that citizens seek in political activity3. Thus, given the context we have described, given the importance of such an irreparable disorder, and given that the right to appeal is not subordinate to the slowness of the justice process, it appears to the court that it is necessary, as a safeguard measure, to make the ineligibility sentence provisionally applicable. (…)

As a final note, at the time, Marine Le Pen was not happy about the law regarding corrupt politicians. In 2013, she said (my translation):

I have heard the President say that those who have been convicted for corruption or tax evasion should be barred from running in elections for life — and so far I fully agree, and it was in my presidential platform. But why not the rest? Why not for favoritism? Why not for embezzling public funds? Why not for fake employee schemes?

So 2013 Le Pen considers the 2025 judgement against her to be laxist.

1 Don't be mislead by the party's name: “radical” in French politics doesn't mean extremist. It means that the party traces its roots to the late 19th century coalition that radically insisted on a republican regime. That coalition's stance on economic policies ranged from ultraliberalism to socialism. By the 1990s, MRG was the part that found the parti radical too liberal, but didn't want to be known as “socialist” or “communist” like the major left-wing parties.

2 i.e. applicable immediately, without waiting for an appeal decision.

3 Earlier, the judgment discussed the fact that the law was revised to make ineligibility an automatic penalty. This does not apply since the facts under trial predate the harsher law, but the court can take their perception of the intent behind the law into account when deciding whether to apply an optional penalty.

query:
Has Russia ever explained its U-turn on going to war with Ukraine?

In January 2022, Russia denied it had plans to attack Ukraine:

Russia is not going to attack Ukraine, said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. “You claim that we are going to attack Ukraine, although we have already explained many times that this is not so,” he said after talks with US Secretary of State Antony Blinken.

A month later, they attacked Ukraine, starting the invasion and subsequent war. Irrespective of whether it had prior intentions to invade Ukraine or not, has Russia ever explicitly acknowledged this change of heart, and if so, what justifications did it give for doing so?
gold_answers:
Russia did not formally explain its U-turn on going to war with Ukraine.

Doing so would have been embarrassing. It would be effectively admitting to having repeatedly lied to the entire world at the highest levels of the Russian government. Instead, we have to look for clues elsewhere, most importantly in Russian President Vladimir Putin's own speeches. In his address to the nation on February 24, 2022, Putin cited multiple reasons for the large-scale invasion of Ukraine. Most of these reasons were long-standing. That is, these reasons existed for a long time prior to the numerous denials of the pending large-scale invasion of Ukraine.

I found one reason that appeared immediately before the start of the large-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is the unanimous ratification by the Russia’s State Duma on February 22, 2022 of the treaties on friendship, cooperation and mutual assistance with the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics (DPR and LPR). This ratification gave the final "justification" for the war - nominally, to protect the ethnic Russians in these pseudo-states from the (non-existent) "genocide" by Ukraine. The notion of genocide had long been falsely spread by the Russian propagandists on state-controlled Russian TV prior to that time. The ratification of the treaty simply gave the formal green light for the invasion.

References:

In the early hours of Thursday, February 24, 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin addressed his nation, announcing a “special military operation” against Ukraine.

The speech came on the heels of his decision to recognise the Donetsk People’s Republic and Luhansk People’s Republic on February 21 and the signing of mutual cooperation agreements between Russia and the two breakaway regions.

Below are highlights translated by Al Jazeera staff based on the transcript, released by the Russian presidency:
...
“We have been left no other option to protect Russia and our people, but for the one that we will be forced to use today. The situation requires us to take decisive and immediate action. The people’s republics of Donbas turned to Russia with a request for help.

“In this regard, in accordance with Article 51 of Part 7 of the UN Charter, with the approval of the Federation Council of Russia and in pursuance of the treaties of friendship and mutual assistance ratified by the Duma on February 22 with the Donetsk People’s Republic and the Luhansk People’s Republic, I decided to launch a special military operation.

"‘No other option’: Excerpts of Putin’s speech declaring war", Al Jazeera, 24 Feb 2022

MOSCOW, February 22. /TASS/. Russia’s State Duma on Tuesday unanimously ratified the treaties on friendship, cooperation and mutual assistance with the Donetsk and Lugansk people’s republics (DPR and LPR), submitted by President Vladimir Putin. The Russian head of state declared the recognition of their sovereignty on Monday. The legislators introduced amendments to the laws on ratification saying the treaties were effective as of the moment of their publication.

The legislators gave the results of the voting a standing ovation.

"The bills are now forwarded to the Federation Council for our colleagues to consider. The president will then decide the future of ratification," State Duma speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said.

Putin signed the treaties with the heads of the Donbass republics - Denis Pushilin and Leonid Pasechnik. The agreements are identical.
