query:
How come Canada is retaliating against US tariffs now instead of after upcoming elections?

My understanding is that, in democratic countries, if there is a looming election, there is also an expectation that the government will not implement major new policies until after the election (example) when the new leader can say they got a mandate from the voters.

Given that, why is Canada retaliating against US tariffs now instead of after the upcoming elections? Trudeau (currently the Canadian prime minister) is probably not going to be prime minister within a few days' time, while the next Canadian federal election is due in several months, as well.

Only thing I can think of is that retaliatory tariffs has broad consensus across all Canadian politicians. However, even then, it seems expected that the new leader should get to decide what to tax, by how much, etc.
gold_answers:
The "caretaker convention" is only triggered after the Governor General dissolves Parliament and calls for a general election. During that period, it is a constitutional convention that only routine operations of government are taken. Although, even within that period, if there is urgent action required in the public interest, the government may take it, especially with consent of other parties.

An election that would trigger the caretaker convention is not "looming." It is simply a popular expectation that when Parliament resumes, the current government will soon thereafter lose a confidence vote. That expectation is not a sufficient trigger for the caretaker convention in Canadian constitutional practice, nor is an internal party process for selecting its new leader.

If Parliament is not dissolved early, the next general election set by the Canada Elections Act is October 20, 2025 — more than 7.5 months from now.

query:
Differences between "snap" and regularly scheduled elections for the electorate and for the politicians?

A comment below When a coalition government like Germany's fails, how is a "snap" election supposed to fix it? (Explain it like I'm five)

I think you are too hung up on the “snap” part. A snap election is just an election. Do you understand how election in a democracy helps forming the government? Being “snap” just means it happens earlier than originally scheduled, there is no other difference.

I do understand "how election in a democracy helps forming the government" but I do not feel "hung up" on anything. Rather than use comments for a discussion, I think a new question is the right place to highlight differences between "snap" and scheduled elections.

In democratic elections, what are the major differences between "snap" federal elections, and regularly scheduled federal elections (e.g. every 4 or 5 years) from the point of view of the electorate, the politicians, and the associated industries (journalism, polling, etc.)?

Answers might include references to things like time, money, and fatigue.
gold_answers:
There are different reasons for snap elections in different systems:

  • The government may be able to call for snap elections whenever it feels like it, likely because they see a political benefit. Such an election comes on short notice, and it would be called because the government does see a benefit.
    So from the point of view of government politicians, there would be a relatively benign political situation making things easier, while the opposite applies to the opposition. Media and the voters may be part of this climate.
  • The political system may require snap elections to resolve gridlock, e.g. when a government does not have the confidence of the parliament (in a parliamentary system). If the government used to have this confidence and lost it between elections, then some faction of parliament changed their opinion and the government can call on the electorate to "ratify" this and help resolve the gridlock at the same time.
    From the point of view of the government, this was either forced on them or it is a desperate gamble to restore failing fortunes. For the opposition, it is an earlier than anticipated chance to get a majority.

It seems impossible to generalize about finances because systems are so different. In Germany, parties get public funds after the election depending on their number of votes, so success in a snap election partly pays for itself.

Neither is it possible to generalize about the voters. Some are exasperated to be innundated by campaigning again, others relish the chance to change the government early.

query:
Are/were counter-tariffs against USA targetting certain products?

I believe it was said that during the previous Trump "trade wars" during 2016-2020, most notably against China, it was said that other countries were responding with targeted counter-tariffs, picking out certain products in particular. The aim was supposedly to cause of loss of job opportunities not just for the average US citizen but for typical Trump voters in particular, in order to make Trump's tariffs backfire as hard as possible.

query:
Are/what makes German parliamentary elections harder to organize than French ones?

On the eve of the European parliamentary election on June 09, 2024, French president Macron called a snap election for the National Assembly. It was held three/four weeks later. (First round on June 30, second round July 7.)

On November 06, 2024, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz fired his finance minister, effectively ending the coalition with the latter's party and thus losing the support of a majority in parliament, but announced he would not resign and only put forward a motion of confidence, required for dissolving parliament and scheduling a new election, in January, leading to a new election in March, because having an election earlier would be impractical. Amid criticism of that approach, the Federal Returning Officer (Bundeswahlleiterin) also warned of "uncalculable risks" should elections be held as "early" as late January or early February (source in German).

I realize Germany's mixed direct/proportional representation system takes more effort in putting together candidate lists for the proportional part, as does collecting signatures for ballot access for smaller/new parties, but most of the issues cited are organizational (ballot printing, finding election officials...). What specific issues allow France to organize elections within three weeks but might prevent Germany from doing so with 9+ weeks advance notice?
gold_answers:
What you are really asking about is comparing the processes applied in Germany and France. I suspect the number of people that really have an overview of the adminstrative details in both is relatively small.

I can only answer from the viewpoint of knowing the processes in Germany, and look at French laws and ordonances and try to spot obvious differences that may account for the slower preparations in Germany. I really beg those readers who are knowledgable about the situation in France to correct my erroneous assumptions.

I'll leave out of my answer the complexity of compiling party lists, as you have pointed at them yourself, and the special circumstances of working around the christmas season.

Election officials

Each polling station in Germany is headed by a committee of at least six persons: a chairman and deputy chairman, a secretary and deputy secretary, and at least two auxilliaries.

All of them have to be found among the electorate by the local returning officer. The main method is calling for volunteers among the public and contacting everyone who has done the job in the past. As an incentive, a small renumeration for the work (federal: 40 Euro) is offered, people working for the state can instead take a half day off. – As a result, working as an election official is relatively popular among teachers.

Theoretically, it would be possible for the returning officer to pick helpers from the electorate at random and enroll them forcibly. But this is considered the very last resort, as no-one gains if they do not show up, or are not motivated to do the job properly.

All in all, gathering the required number of officials, which amount to roundabout 0.5% of the electorate, is a tenacious process.

Also, since none of the officials are professional adminstrators, training them for their function is crucial. Dates have to be found for these training sessions, with reasonable advance notices. I don't have an overview for other states, but I know in Berlin all chairmen, secretaries and their deputies have to take part. For each electoral constituency (200.000 voters on average), around 20 sessions with 50+ attendants are typically scheduled, spread out over two weeks.

Looking at the ordonance governing the work of election officials in France, the process is noticably leaner. Each polling station is headed by at least four persons, "a chairman, at least two assessors and a secretary chosen by them from among the electors of the municipality."

The mayor of the commune, his adjuncts and the members of the city council are required to fill the chairmen roles. Only if their number is depleted, other members of the electorate will be choosen. Each candidate has the right to name one assessor and one substitute for each polling station, choosen from the electorate of the whole département, and if the required number is not met, the mayor of the commune can name a member of the city council to fill in.

France is more rural than Germany, and a lot of communes are much smaller. Accordingly, the number of mayors and city councils is much higher. That helps, but especially in larger cities it is not enough. The chairmen and secretaries get a renummeration for their work (200+ Euro). But parties struggle to name assessors, who are expected to work for free. Consequently, some cities have started to offer money to motivate citizens to become assessors.

Conclusion: France seems to have found a mode where aquiring election officials is not without difficulties, but at least partial solutions are offered by law. In Germany by contrast, the returning officers are left alone with that headache. Each and every election campaign is accompanied by public appearances of the returning officers begging for helpers, and stating that a mere three weeks before election day, they are still seeking thousands of volunteers.

Returning officers

In Germany, the local organisation of elections is based on the 298 electoral constituencies. Each district has one committee to oversee proceedings, and one returning officer (with a temporary office of maybe 10 employees). He may be able to also activate additional capacities for organisation from the communes the constituency spans, but basically everything that needs to be done locally is his responsibility.

In France, the local organisation is based on the communes, which act in their own right. There are 35,000 collectivités, each with a mayor (maire), (at least some) staff, and a council (conseil municipal). They all can be activated for elections, and have the needed authority to organise things.

Conclusion: The French way of spreading out the work to a large number of small units might for elections well be more efficient than the German federalism, which on a sub-state level is often characterized by each administrative level guarding his jurisdiction jealously.

Vote invitation

In Germany, each elector is sent a card or letter inviting him/her to take part in an election. These notices are prepared from the voters registers, and contain not only the address of the polling station the voter should present themselves at, but also a number for finding their entry in the register.

Preparing these invitations requires the assignment of the voters to precincts and their respective polling station, and the location of the stations to be known. While in general not much changes from election to election, both requirements are formally prepared for each election separately.

In France, as far as I can make out, no invitation to an individual election is sent. Instead, voters are issued a polling card (Carte d'électeur) valid for multiple elections. This card assigns them a precinct, notes the location of the polling station and certifies their inscription in the voters register.

The reason why the assignment can be done this way is because the distribution of the voters to precincts are prepared independently of election dates. The mayor of each commune publishes a list of precincts and their respective polling stations on a yearly basis.

Conclusion: The French method of treating precinct assignment and the waiving of sending individual invitations removes a major time limit.

Ballots

In Germany, there is one ballot containing the names of all candidates, and voting consists of ticking a box. The ballots are printed by the returning officer, who obviously is dependent on the parties and candidates providing the needed names in a timely fashion.

In France, the procedure was described by user Relaxed, thanks for that. Each candidate or party has to take care of printing his/her own ballot (they can get the costs reimbursed by the state but they have to make sure they are printed in time to be distributed by mail and to all polling stations). Voting consists of choosing one of these standardized papers and putting it in a small envelope. Ballots and optionally an acompaigning leaflet can be sent as a package prepared by the city to the voters, if they are available in time. If the ballots are not provided early enough, voters can pick them at the polling station. It's not uncommon for the ballots from small / fringe candidates to be missing on election day. But even then they are not excluded from the election. As long as they met the deadline to register, if someone somehow comes up with a valid ballot, it should be tallied and reported.

Conclusion: I am hard pressed to decide whether it is faster to collect information and print them up centrally, or to print decentralized, and then collect papers. What will be in favor of the French method is the very pragmatic handling of deadlines: either you come up with the ballot until election day, or no one can vote for you.

Postal voting

In Germany, postal voting (or early voting by requesting, receiving and filling out the postal voting forms and ballots at city hall in one go) is a popular form of voting, used by up to a third of the electorate. In case of a snap election, the timeline for postal voting may be abridged, but it still has to be made available.

France has no postal voting, except for expatriates. Everyone has to show up at the polling station on election day, or authorize a mandatee to vote in his/her place.

The TV magazin Karambolage has made a video (in French, in German) comparing the German postal vote ("Briefwahl") to the French authorization ("Procuration").

query:
How would submission deadlines be applied to elections following a failed Vertrauensfrage?

Germany has a unique way of dissolving parliament. If the chancellor loses a vote of confidence, the president can dissolve the Bundestag within 21 days, which would lead to elections within 60 days.

Given that the Bundespräsident could dissolve the Bundestag immediately after the vote of confidence has been lost, you could theoretically have new elections less than 60 days later.

However, elections have deadlines. §19 BWahlG specifies that candidates for constituencies and candidate lists for the states have to be submitted by 6 pm on the 69th day before the election.
If a non-established party wants to run in the election they have to declare that by the 97th day before the election, which would be an impossible deadline even if the president took the maximum amount of time.

How do people run in these elections, given the fact that it may be impossible to declare your candidacy after it is announced that the election is even happening?
gold_answers:
TL;DR: §52(3)

(3) Das Bundesministerium des Innern und für Heimat wird ermächtigt, im Falle einer Auflösung des Deutschen Bundestages die in dem Bundeswahlgesetz und in der Bundeswahlordnung bestimmten Fristen und Termine durch Rechtsverordnung ohne Zustimmung des Bundesrates abzukürzen.

So the ministry of the interior is allowed to shorten the deadlines in case of an unscheduled new election without the approval of the governments of the federal states (Bundesrat).

Here is for example how that looked like in case of the 2005 election: https://www.bundestag.de/resource/blob/535006/5c4e8b62072752bed322b3e0bf61fc0c/WD-3-192-17-pdf.pdf

But apparently this norm was overruled in 2016 so there needs to be a new one.

Also no, the president can not immediately dissolve the Bundestag (German parliament).

Dissolving parliament is a tricky issue, especially given it's frequent abuse in the declining Weimar Republic, where "Presidential cabinets" ruled for much of the later period, where the president dissolved parliament and appointed a lame duck government which ruled largely by laws crafted via executive orders of the president, while the parliament was absent. So the rights of the president to dissolve parliament have been majorly restricted and deadlines are set to keep that vacancy period short.

Apparently this is set in articles 63, 67 and 68 of the constitution.

Essentially 63 (german) allows for dissolution of parliament if no chancellor is elected in the first place. So usually the president proposes the most likely chancellor, biggest faction, leader of a coalitions, etc then a vote is held, if that votes fails parliament itself can propose a candidate and if that one fails as well to achieve a majority of MPs as well, then the president can dissolve and schedule new elections.

Article 67 (german) allows for parliament itself to rid itself of a chancellor, how such a vote of no confidence MUST be concurrent with the election of a new chancellor (who would need to get the majority). So parliament can no dissolve itself.

Unless (article 68 (german) the chancellor poses a vote of confidence where he aims to get the approval of a majority of parliament (usually the members of his own coalition suffice for that) and if that vote of confidence is lost the president can dissolve parliament within 21 days unless the other parties jump in an elect a new chancellor with a majority.

So as a chancellor was elected by a majority article 63 no longer applies. Meaning either the rest of parliament needs to form a new majority coalition (which is unlikely). So the current government can stay in office unless they themselves create a vote of confidence in order to make space for new elections. And apparently the government has scheduled that question to be raised on the 15th of January 2025. So in terms of practical problems the other parties have time to prepare for that in advance while the official dead lines are likely to be placed within the constraints of the 60 days via a norm issued by the government.

Edit: Also while the president dissolving parliament doesn't shorten the 60 days, the 60 days still are an upper limit so they could do it faster if they wanted to. Though there could also be limits with regards to how fast exactly, for example the time between a proposing a vote of no confidence and having the vote is for 2 days or explicitly 48 hours actually.

query:
Has there ever been a comprehensive audit of voter eligibility and identity in a U.S. election?

I'm well aware that there have been numerous recounts in U.S. elections (most notably the 2000 recount in Florida). They sometimes find small discrepancies from non-malicious human errors but otherwise show that votes are being counted accurately. However, recounts can only validate vote counting accuracy - they cannot check whether the votes themselves were legitimate.

Have there been any comprehensive, large-scale audits that checked other sources of possible fraud? Specifically:

  • Voter qualification: Confirming each voter's citizenship and residency status at the time of the election
  • Ballot authenticity: Ensuring voters cast their own ballots, including checking if each voter was alive on Election Day, their identity wasn't misused, and their mail ballot wasn't submitted by others without permission
  • Assisted voting integrity: Checking whether those requiring assistance could select their preferred candidate without improper influence

Has such an audit been completed in recent decades? If multiple such audits have been completed, what was the largest election (by votes cast) to undergo this scrutiny? I'll also accept answers covering audits that used random sampling or other optimizations rather than checking every single vote.

Update from Nov 1st: Reports from routine voter roll maintenance or voters list purges would qualify if thoroughly documented. Here's a purely hypothetical example of the kinds of checks and findings such a pre-voting report might include:

Check Type % of Total Check Type % of Total
Total Registered Voters 100% Birth Date Mismatch with SSA 1.24%
Address Has >8 Voters 0.82% Multiple State Registrations 2.15%
Commercial Zone Listed as Residence 0.31% Failed Citizenship Check 0.08%
Deceased Voter Match 0.67% Referred for Investigation 0.007%

Such an audit would need to detail its complete methodology, databases used (SSA, DHS, DMV, etc.), how their verification processes work, how they've been improving it over the years, etc.

Answering a follow-up question from the comments:

How many occurrences of significant fraud have been observed in other high-functioning Western democracies in the last century or so?

  • In 2005, there were credible reports of electoral fraud involving postal voting in Birmingham, UK
  • In 2011, a voter suppression scandal occurred in Canada, where the election in Etobicoke Centre (Ontario) was decided by a 26-vote margin. Allegedly, 181 voters were improperly allowed to vote, but the Canadian Supreme Court upheld the result in a split 4-3 decision
  • The 2016 Austrian Presidential election was annulled and re-run due to irregularities, particularly with postal votes

And some U.S. examples for the sake of completeness:

  • The 1982 Illinois State Senate Primary saw numerous instances of fraud, with a grand jury finding approximately 100,000 fraudulent votes cast in Chicago. Fifty-eight election officials were convicted of various election-related offenses
  • The 1997 Miami mayoral election was annulled due to absentee ballot fraud
  • The 2003 East Chicago mayoral Democratic primary was overturned because of absentee ballot fraud
  • The 2018 North Carolina's 9th Congressional District election was annulled due to illegal ballot harvesting and ballot tampering
gold_answers:
I think you're somewhat misusing terms here. Risk-limiting audits are conducted for some US elections. Typically these involve checking if a sample of the ballots were counted properly (as opposed to a recount, where the whole lot would be counted again).

While the phrase "postelection audit" can be used to mean a variety of election validation efforts, as a term of art it refers to checking paper ballots (or records) against the results produced by the vote tallying equipment to ensure accuracy.

Some details:

A total of 49 states conduct some type of post-election audit. Alabama does not require post-election audits but piloted different audit types in the 2022 election.

The most common type is a “traditional” post-election tabulation audit. There are also risk-limiting audits (RLAs), procedural audits, and audits that states conduct after an election that do not fall into either of these categories. More details on each type of audit are found below, but in summary:

  • 35 states and Washington, D.C., require a traditional post-election tabulation audit: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Ohio, Oregon, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana (upon implementation of a new voting system), Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Of these, Ohio, Oregon and Washington give counties the option of conducting a risk-limiting audit instead and Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Texas, have had pilot programs to conduct risk-limiting audits.

  • Six states have a statutory requirement for a risk-limiting audit: Georgia, Colorado, Maine, (pilot in 2024 and statewide in 2025), Nevada, Rhode Island, and Virginia.

  • Eight states have other post-election audits that do not fall into the categories above:

    • Indiana (procedural and/or traditional post-election audits may be authorized under some circumstances, with a pilot for RLAs)
    • Michigan (traditional is authorized but not required, procedural audit, and had a pilot program for an RLA in 2020) Mississippi (procedural audit)
    • Nebraska (not required but may be requested by the secretary of state)
    • New Hampshire (randomized audit of ballot counting devices)
    • North Dakota (post-election logic and accuracy test)
    • Oklahoma (traditional is authorized but not required) South Carolina (data comparison)

Traditional post-election tabulation audits are the most common audit type and look at a fixed percentage of voting districts or voting machines and compare the paper record to the results produced by the voting system. Even in a landslide election, they will count the same number of ballots as they would in a nail-biter election. Traditional post-election tabulation audits are usually conducted manually by hand-counting a portion of the paper records and comparing them to the electronic results produced by an electronic voting machine.

In recent years, researchers have developed statistically based audit techniques that decrease the number of ballots to be audited, while also providing statistical confidence that the election result is correct. This method checks a sample of ballots (or voter verifiable records) that is guaranteed to have a large, pre-specified chance of correcting the reported outcome if the reported outcome is wrong (that is, if a full hand count would reveal an outcome different from the reported outcome). As defined in Washington, "a 'risk-limiting audit' means an audit protocol that uses statistical principles and methods and is designed to limit the risk of certifying an incorrect election outcome." In races with a large margin, fewer ballots need to be counted. If the race is tighter, more ballots are audited.

States may have a process for ensuring the correct process and procedures were followed during the course of the election. This is referred to as a “procedural audit” and may be conducted instead of or in addition to a post-election tabulation audit. Procedural audits vary in their scope and comprehensiveness, but almost always include a ballot accounting and reconciliation process.

In 2023, Utah passed a law requiring biennial procedural audits in addition to their traditional audit. The procedural audit is conducted by the Legislative Auditor General and may include auditing voter registration processes, candidate filing, ballot preparation and more.

As you can see, checking the eligibility of the voters after they cast their votes is seldom done as part of these audits, although perhaps Utah wants to change that.

I managed to find what Utah enacted (wrt voters' audit):

(2) The audit shall include: (a) a random selection of at least .02% of the active registered voters statewide (b) at least one active registered voter from each county. (3) For each voter selected for the audit, the auditor shall: (a) verify that the voter is eligible for registration; (b) verify that the voter's registration information is accurate and supported by the documentation on file; (c) verify that there is a signature on file for the voter; (d) check for duplicate voter registrations; and (e) search available resources to determine whether the voter is deceased.

So, the mandatory sampled percentage in each audit is pretty low (0.02%). N.B. it's officially called a "voter registration audit". TBH, IDK how it's different from the "purges" you've mentioned other than by name, and perhaps periodicity. Actually, the Utah audit doesn't seem to mandate removing somebody from the rolls. Just that the audit need result in a report identifying areas of concern. But presumably removing ineligible entries could be a follow-up action. So I guess that's the difference between an audit and a purge. So, states which conduct regular purges, and in which citizens need to re-prove their citizenship, implicity do such (voter as opposed to vote) audits.

By the way, most of your examples don't pertain to elections annulled because of unqualified voters, but rather due to other kinds of irregularities/fraud.

As for the Canadian example, it's somewhat less clear than you make it. The first instance appeal was successful on the grounds that records of voter eligibility were lost or misplaced by the state. It wasn't actually proven in court those people were not actually eligible to vote. So the Supreme Court erred on the side of not disqualifying votes because of a possible clerical error on behalf of (temp) state employees.

In the US, non-citizen residents who register to vote are sometimes prosecuted. I'm not aware of an election where the (proven) number of these was high enough to change a result. The DA statement even stuff like:

Noncitizen voting is an extremely isolated and rare event. Investigations in multiple states and nationwide have found no evidence of large numbers of noncitizens registering to vote. Even less common is a noncitizen actually casting a ballot.

Conversely:

Election officials must be careful not to mistakenly remove eligible voters from voter rolls, since some databases may be outdated and may not show if an immigrant has become a naturalized citizen. Such errors resulted in large numbers of eligible citizens wrongly flagged for removal in Texas in 2019. [...]

After the 2016 election, the Brennan Center for Justice, which advocates for voting rights, surveyed local election officials in 42 jurisdictions with high immigrant populations and found just 30 cases of suspected noncitizens voting out of 23.5 million votes cast, or 0.0001%. [...]

While the conservative Heritage Foundation has actively promoted claims about the risk of noncitizens voting this campaign season, its own data suggests how rare these cases are. The Washington Post reviewed a Heritage database of voter fraud cases and found 85 cases relating to allegations of noncitizens voting between 2002 and 2023. [...] That analysis found only 10 cases involving undocumented immigrants since the 1980s. Heritage has said the database is just a sampling of fraud cases and is not comprehensive.

Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger launched an audit in 2022 that found over the previous 25 years, fewer than 1,700 people believed to be noncitizens had attempted to register to vote. None were able to cast ballots.

The last bit refers to 2020 only. It is claimed a few [may] have voted before:

Georgia’s top elections official said Wednesday that a check of voter rolls found that 20 of the 8.2 million people registered to vote in the state are not U.S. citizens.

Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said during a news conference that the voter registrations for those people had been canceled and that they will be referred to local prosecutors for potential criminal charges. His office said none of those people has cast a ballot in November’s general election, but nine of the 20 had voted in previous elections and the other 11 had no record of voting.

Additionally, there are 156 people whose citizenship status requires additional investigation and his office has opened case files for those individuals, Raffensperger said.

TBH, if I'm not misreading that piece, the claim of non-citizenship appears to be based mainly on the fact that they "had filled out a sworn statement saying they were not citizens to get out of jury duty". As this is a recent announcement, we'll see how the actual prosecutions turn out. (From another survey, about 9% of Americans apparently claim to have lied to get out of jury duty. The vast majority of these gave other reasons than non-citizenship though.)

BTW, it's been alleged that the Georgia voter audit in some cases violated their own guidelines that require someone to have affirmed somewhere they're non-citizen after voting, but in some cases a voter's affirmation prior to the election was used as "proof" of non-citizenship (so even if they could have acquired it in the meantime, which some say they did).

There have also been some controversial surveys that (simply) asked respondents if they were non-citizen and have voted. The results of these have been contested on the grounds of respondent carelessness, i.e. margin of error in surveys.

The latter is probably (the two or three kinds of) data being called an "investigation" but they're clearly not election audits, nor does it make a lot of sense to call them that.

Also, regarding purges, the decision to not vote is often used a trigger.

query:
Has any mass protest in the USA after 1945 successfully pressured the government to change its decision based on the protesters' demands?

As far as I recall, several mass protests took place in the USA against the Vietnam War, and the government quelled them using violent means, such as the Kent State shooting, etc.

Has any mass protest in the USA after 1945 successfully pressured the government to change its decision based on the protesters' demands?
gold_answers:
Has any mass protest in the USA after 1945 successfully pressured the government to change its decision based on the protesters' demands?

One single mass protest? Probably not. It takes a concerted, long-term effort to change behaviors (and laws).

That said, the civil rights movement from the late 1940s to the late 1960s certainly qualifies. The protests ranged from very small scale (e.g., Rosa Parks) to very large scale (e.g., the August 1963 March on Washington). The cumulative effects of these protests included executive orders, Supreme Court decisions, and federal legislative acts.

query:
Is or was there ever a US poll how many Americans support bombing Irans's nuclear facilities?

Recently:

Republican White House hopeful Donald Trump said he believed Israel should strike Iran’s nuclear facilities in response to the Islamic Republic’s recent missile barrage.

[...Biden's] “answer should have been, hit the nuclear first, and worry about the rest later,” Trump added.

(Interestingly, Trump finally agrees with Bolton on that, whom of course has himself reiterated that point recently too.)

Are or were there any polls in the US about this, now or ever before, whether Iran's nuclear facilities should be bombed, either by the US or with US blessing?
gold_answers:
There is an August 2022 poll from The Chicago Council on Global Affairs/Ipsos addressing exactly your question here.

A minority of Americans would support the use of force to destroy Iran’s nuclear facilities if it restarted development of a nuclear weapon: 46 percent would support air strikes and 38 percent would support the deployment of US troops.

It’s worth noting that this is a large amount of support in the post-2016 era of American foreign policy for US intervention, and digging into the poll one even finds that it’s concentrated on the right:

Republicans are about 15 to 20 percentage points more likely than Democrats or Independents to support the US government launching cyberattacks or airstrikes against Iran. GOP supporters are also significantly more likely than either group to support sending troops to destroy the country’s nuclear facilities (+12 percentage points compared to Democrats, +18 percentage points to Independents).

In a 2019, FiveThirtyEight noted that Americans are more in favor of using troops in Iran in case of them obtaining a nuclear weapon than in an any other case, including an invasion of a NATO ally or of Taiwan by China.

…a survey conducted in June found that the use of military force in Iran may be one military intervention that the U.S. public could get behind, especially if Americans perceive Iran’s nuclear capabilities as a threat. In that survey, which was released earlier this month by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, 70 percent of respondents, including 82 percent of Republicans and 66 percent of Democrats, supported using U.S. troops to stop Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.

In a 2012 poll, 53% - 56% of Americans supported such strikes.

query:
Were US men and women ever so divided in national polls?

Reportedly

The numbers are stunning. An NBC poll this week found men favour Trump over Harris by 12 points, 52% to 40%. Among women, Harris leads Trump by 21 points: 58% to 37%. Put the two together and you have a gender chasm of 33 points. Men may not be from Mars and women may not be from Venus, but when it comes to choosing a US president, they are on different planets.

Is the number cherry picked? Is it historically unprecedented in US politics?
gold_answers:
Yes, this is the largest divide between men and women in polling data for a presidential election that I can find1 demographic polling results for, and the previous maximum was 2020.

The columnist in that article has made a mistake in reporting the sum of the two gender gaps, one for Trump and one for Harris, as one "gender gap". The academic definition is the gap for the leading or winning candidate.

[% Women for Leading or Winning Candidate] – [% Men for Leading or Winning Candidate] = Gender Gap

For the current polling, that would be the 18 point difference for Harris, rather than the combined 18 + 15 for Harris + Trump.

Both the academic definition, and this author's method, agree that 2024 is the widest divide between the voting patterns of men and women.

  1. I can only find polling data split by gender going back to 1976 before there starts to be gaps, so there may have been a point between 1920 and 1976 where there was an equal, or larger gap, but I don't know of it.

query:
Which Lebanese politicians, in the 2023-24 violence cycle, had called upon Hezbollah not to persist in attacking Israel from Lebanese soil?

Pretty much what the title says. One can be shocked at the numbers of deaths in Lebanon, reported to be nearly 500 two days ago, and still note that Israeli towns have been been getting targeted for almost a year and that 60000 people had to be evacuated.

Many countries would not put up with that indefinitely - and Israel is not known for its pusillanimity and infinite patience, not even under less controversial war leadership than Netanyahu's - and the Lebanese establishment must have known Hezbollah was eventually going to provoke an escalated response.

Since Hezbollah is not running Lebanon, and since it is drawn only from the Shiite components of Lebanese society, have non-Hezbollah/non-Shiite Lebanese politicians called on it to stand back/stand down?

I am mostly interested in statements before the last two weeks, as attacks from other countries are known to have a rallying effect in most case.

On the other hand, I know that in the more distant past, politicians had stated Lebanon was not ready for another war. This Q really is more about the last 6 months or so, as violence persisted. To put it another way: it is one thing to muse in the abstract about the undesirability of Hezbollah starting another war, before Hezbollah is shooting. It is another to call on Hezbollah to stop shooting when it has started to do so.

Gaza is another question entirely. The rights, and wrongs, of Israeli actions in Gaza are not the rights, and wrongs, of Israeli action against Hezbollah. It is also not about the rights and wrongs of Israeli treatment of the Palestinians. Neither is this question supporting, or criticizing, the methods used by Israel to strike at Hezbollah, as of the time it was asked.

This question is exclusively asking about what Lebanese politicians said about the wisdom, to Lebanese interests, of attacking Israel.

If those politicians base their arguments on Gaza and/or Palestinians, sure, that is in the scope of the question.

see also: ethnic/religious demographics of Lebanon in 2022
gold_answers:
TLDR: I'm not a regular observer of Lebanese politics, but it seems to me by surveying the statements of a few most notorious politicians there that except Christian leaders everyone else's (Sunni, Druze, not-officially-Hezbollah Shia) is either turning a blind [rhetorical] eye to Hezbollah's doings and just blaming Israel for everything, and/or actively endorsing Hezbollah's "unified arena" vision of the conflict.

At least some Christian parties (not a negligible entity in Lebanon) have called for moves that are more or less similar to the US plan.

May 1, 2024. The leader of a main Christian political party in Lebanon blasted the Shiite militant group Hezbollah for opening a front with Israel to back up its ally Hamas, saying it has harmed Lebanon without making a dent in Israel’s crushing offensive in the Gaza Strip.

In an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday night, Samir Geagea of the Lebanese Forces Party said Hezbollah should withdraw from areas along the border with Israel and the Lebanese army should deploy in all points where militants of the Iran-backed group have taken positions.

[...] “All the damage that could have happened in Gaza ... happened. What was the benefit of military operations that were launched from south Lebanon? Nothing,” Geagea said, pointing the the death toll and massive destruction in Lebanon’s border villages.

Not coincidentally, Christians in Lebanon have the highest level of faith in the US.

Even the leader of the FPM, which is a Christian party that was traditionally allied with Hezbollah, advanced some criticism (sometime around March):

"The main problem that arose recently was crossing the limits of defending Lebanon and getting involved in a conflict in which we cannot make decisions," FPM head Gebran Bassil said.

Nonetheless, at about the same time Bassil was making ouvertures to Hezbollah, for a renewed political alliance, but also blaming Hezbollah for the fracture:

According to him, it was Hezbollah that "left the agreement when it abandoned the principle of state-building, the partnership with the FPM, and broke the ceiling of protecting Lebanon."

But words (especially from an opposition party) don't stop missiles. And the Lebanese Armed forces, which enjoy a high level of popularity in Lebanon (see previous link) have done nothing. The present central government is more affiliated with Syria, IIRC.

(Sunni) PM Mikati has been quite more vague on this, e.g.

24 October 2023

Mikati paid a surprise trip to southern Lebanon on Tuesday, as Israel and the terror group — a key Hamas ally — continued to trade deadly cross-border fire, while Israel and its Western allies have repeatedly warned the group against an escalation.

[...] During his visit, the caretaker prime minister emphasized what he said was Lebanon’s commitment to UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the 2006 Second Lebanon War. That resolution called for the demilitarization in southern Lebanon of all groups other than state security forces. [...]

“We came to the beloved south… to reaffirm peace-loving Lebanon’s respect for all legitimate international resolutions and its commitment to implementing” resolution 1701, Mikati said, according to a statement.

So, yeah, words about commitment to UN stuff. OTOH he's used far stronger terms in denouncing Israel:

“The continuing Israeli aggression on Lebanon is a war of extermination in every sense of the word and a destructive plan that aims to destroy Lebanese villages and towns,” Mikati told a cabinet meeting. He urged “the United Nations and the General Assembly and influential countries... to deter the (Israeli) aggression.”

Likewise, words about the "resistance doing its duty" that can easily be interpreted as moral support for Hezbollah.

“We are always advocates of peace, and our choice is the choice of peace and the implementation of UN Resolution 1701. It is incumbent upon Israel to cease its repeated attacks on Lebanon and halt the war in Gaza, with everyone adhering to UN Resolution 2735,” Mikati stated.

He continued: “The resistance is doing its duty, and the Lebanese government is doing its duty, and our goal is to protect the country in every sense of the word.”

As another Christian politician (Samy Gemayel) put it though, as long as the Sunnis don't take a stronger stance against Hezbollah, any concrete [Lebanese] efforts against it are likely to turn into sectarian warfare. (And even if the Sunnis did take a stronger rhetorical stance, it's IMHO not a given that Hezbollah can be convinced by words, but we don't really know unless/until that happens.)

Alas the Druze in Lebanon (or at least their most famous politicians) don't seem too inclined to blame Hezbollah for anything, e.g. in late July:

Lebanese Druze leader Walid Jumblatt warned Saturday about Israel’s efforts to “incite strife” in the region after it accused Hezbollah of being involved in the shelling of the town of Druze in Majdal Shams in the occupied Golan Heights.

Jumblatt said in light of Hezbollah’s statement denying any involvement in the attack on Druze, “We reiterate our warning and alertness to what the Israeli enemy has long been working on—to incite strife, fragment the region, and target its components,” as reported by Lebanon’s National News Agency. “We have previously thwarted this (Israeli) scheme, and now that it has reemerged, we remain vigilant alongside the resistance and all fighters confronting Israeli aggression and occupation.”

And about the situation in general, he said:

The armistice agreement dictates that Lebanon and Israel have a certain neutral distance in northern Lebanon as well as Palestine. But implementing the armistice agreement from one side is not logical.

That's pretty close to endorsing Nasrallah's "unity of the arenas".

As for the officially-not-Hezbollah, but still Shiite politicians, like the the Speaker of Parliament, Nabih Berri--don't look for any calls for Hezbollah to disengage there. He was recently (August) praising the wise plans of revenge of the Iran axis, with talk like "revenge is a dish best served cold" etc. He struck a more conciliatory tone recently, after Israel struck back on a large scale.

Or look at his earlier (April) interview in a London paper blaming (just) "Israeli aggression" for "turning most villages and towns situated south of the Litani river into dilapidated and uninhabitable areas" with no mention of any Hezbollah activities.

query:
What explanations can be offered for the extreme see-sawing in Montana's senate race polling?

Glancing at Five Thirty Eight data for Montana's senate race between Testor and Sheehy, the pattern that emerges is summarized (in order of polls closing earlier):

  1. Sheehy, narrow margin (+2, Emerson College);
  2. 6 days later - Sheehy, large margin (+6, APR - Change of 4 points for Sheehy);
  3. 2 days later - Testor, large margin (+5, RMG - Change of 11 points for Testor);
  4. 6 days later - Sheehy, large margin (+7, POS - Change of 12 points for Sheehy).

That's a lot of change packed into a two-week period. Is polling in Montana especially volatile, are there campaign events meaningfully yanking the needle around back and forth, what's the story there?
gold_answers:
Pollster Quality

A major premise of 538 is that all polls are not equally informative. Different polling organizations use different methodologies, and that creates biases within the polls.

So just looking at the 538 Pollster Ratings, you can see that the Emerson College poll is solid - Emerson is ranked 8 out of all the pollsters 538 has graded, with 2.9 stars out of a possible 3.

In contrast, Public Opinion Strategies is significantly lower quality - ranked 139 with 1.7 out of 3.0 stars.

RMG is ranked 60, with 2.3 / 3.0 stars, and I couldn't find APR, though there's a Polling and Research Inc, which is ranked 68, so close to RMG if that's APR under a different name.

Putting all that together with just vibes and no math, I'd say that we throw out the POS poll, weight ourselves towards the high quality Emerson poll, and say "in August it was too close call with perhaps a slight lean R."

query:
Historical U.S. political party "realignments"?

Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., in his interview with Tucker Carlson (@1:17), says:

There's been a bunch of realignments (about 4 or 5) throughout American history; and I think we're going through one right now, with the Democratic Party and with both political parties really changing in a very dramatic way.

What were these "4 or 5" political party "realignments" in U.S. history?
gold_answers:
Theoretical Context

Duverger's law states that subject to certain conditions, a political system with single member district plurality vote candidate elections naturally tends towards having two, roughly equal, political parties.

The United States has this kind of political system and has had two major parties for most of its history except brief transition periods and some false starts towards transitions that didn't come to fruition.

(The exception to Duverger's law, which give the U.K. parliament and Canada multiple political parties with a U.S. style-election single member district plurality winner system is that it mandates two dominant political parties in any one geographic area. This has spawned pro- (and sometimes anti-) separatist/autonomy political parties in Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Quebec, for example, but the U.S. has had two main political parties, apart from transitional periods between political party systems, for essentially all of its history.)

In a two party system, the parties form coalitions of people and platforms acceptable to those people, designed to secure majorities prior to the election, rather than by forming coalitions after the election as parliamentary systems with multiple political parties do. Those coalitions and collections of party platform policies constantly change to give each party a shot at a majority coalition, sometimes gradually, and sometimes not so gradually. There are brief periods when one party gains temporary dominance due to major shifts in the political environment and ideologies, but eventually, things settle down back to two major nearly 50-50 political parties again.

The history of the major political parties and the realignment of the political party system in the United States over time is largely a story of the more dramatic and less gradual shifts in those coalitions and policy leanings in U.S. political history, driven largely by national politics. Many states have spent much longer periods in a dominant period phase, in part, because they are more homogeneous relative to the leading political party divisions at the national level. Federalism in the U.S. has largely prevented each different U.S. state from developing its own political parties that flirt with that 50-50 balance, except by accident when the federal median voter aligns with a state median voter.

A Short History Of U.S. Political Parties

There are up to nine plausible historical events that could constitute a political party re-alignment in the U.S. under the current U.S. Constitution, and I'm not certain which 4-5 were being referred to in this instance. See, in part, here (party divisions in Congress over time).

  1. (not included) The Revolutionary War and Article of Confederation period from 1776 to 1789, prior to the current U.S. Constitution, lacked clear political parties, per se, because the dominant issue was independence from Great Britain and the country was united under the leadership of George Washington, the commander-in-chief of the U.S. military during most of this era.

  2. (arguably) The period without well organized political parties from 1789 to to 1794. This is arguably a pre-political party system rather than a realignment. President George Washington, the hero-leader of the American independence movement and revolutionary war was the President for the first eight years and presided in this time period continuing the unity around independence from Great Britain that prevailed prior to the U.S. Constitution.

  3. (arguably) The Democratic-Republicans party and the Federalist Party from the 1794 election until 1824. This is arguably not a realignment but the starting point of the political party system in the U.S. The Democratic-Republicans favored a weak federal government (and are associated with James Madison and Thomas Jefferson), and the Federalists (most strongly associated with Alexander Hamilton and John Adams) favored a stronger federal government and a national central bank. It emerged as George Washington was on the brink of leaving the political scene removing the unifying factor in the federal government (although the issue of independence from Great Britain, upon which the parties were united, wasn't really fully put to bed until the War of 1812 was concluded).

  4. The replacement of the Democratic-Republicans and the Federalists, with the Jacksonian and Anti-Jackson parties from the 1824 election to 1836. The Jacksonian party was populist and pro-political patronage, the Anti-Jackson party was a "good government" party. Abolition was more a grass roots movement than a political party platform plank of either major political party at this point. The Jacksonian Party was closer to the Democratic-Republican Party, and the Federalist Party was closer to the Anti-Jackson Party, although the coalitions and policy emphasis of the new parties weren't the same.

  5. The replacement of the Jacksonian and Anti-Jackson parties with the Democratic Party and the Whigs from the 1836 election to 1854. The Democratic Party was a Southern pro-slavery party in this time period, while the Whigs were a northern conservative party that tolerated but didn't like slavery. While the coalitions and policy emphasis of the Democratic Party and the Whigs weren't the same, the Democratic Party was basically the successor to the Jacksonian Party and the Whigs were basically the successor to the Anti-Jackson Party.

  6. The creation of the Republican Party in the late 1850s, replacing the Whigs by the 1856 election, with a two year transition period in the 34th Congress following the 1854 election that was muddled and transitional. In this time period, the Republican party was a northern, liberal, abolitionist leaning party (relatively speaking), and the Democratic party was a Southern pro-slavery party. Of course, from 1861-1865, the U.S. Civil War was fought and Republicans dominated Congress and continued to do so during the period after the U.S. Civil War known as Reconstruction, when the formerly Confederate States were reintegrated back in the United States, but post-reconstruction, the Democratic and Republican parties were very similar in ideology and coalitions to the Democratic and Republican Parties that had existed on the eve of the U.S. Civil War. So, while there was a major disruption in the political history of the U.S. at this point, it didn't shuffle the major political parties in the U.S. very much. The Reconstruction period was a "weird" political transition period and dominated by the Republican Party until it ended, nationwide, but didn't have much of a lasting political impact in the former Confederate States. With the slavery issue resolved after the U.S. Civil War and with Reconstruction ended, the Republican party drifted in a conservative direction on economic policy that reached a peak on the eve of the Great Depression (largely ignoring the Jim Crow segregation regime emerging in the South, with an attitude similar to that of the Whigs towards slavery prior to the U.S. Civil War), although its coalition was little changed. In the late 1890s and early 1900s, a third-party progressive movement that tried and largely failed to realign the political party system in the U.S. emerged, favoring temperance, good government, and mostly, more liberal leaning policies, this third-party movement died as the two major parties assimilated key planks of the progressive party platform and then FDR's dominant Democratic party adopted much less incremental economically liberal reforms.

  7. (arguably) The dominant party period during the Great Depression and World War II where the Democratic Party has sustained supermajorities from the 1932 election to 1942. The parties remained the same, but the dominant role of the Democratic Party under President Franklin D. Roosevelt greatly changed the character of the two major parties. Under FDR, the Democratic Party was basically a populist party leaning into being a Western European style Democratic Socialist party, and the Republican party was all but irrelevant at the federal level.

  8. (arguably) The return to a reasonably balanced Republican and Democratic party system in which the Republican party was still northern and urban but had shifted from a liberal party to a center-right party, and the Democratic party which kept strong southern roots (exemplified in the concept of the "Solid South") that was muddied somewhat by the big tent of the dominant party period. This lasted about a decade or two before the process of realignment described in #8 below, eventually took hold in a noticeable way.

  9. If you hear the term "realignment" today, referring to U.S. political parties, the reference is to this process. This is the process by which the Republican Party and the Democratic Party traded ideologies starting around the time of the U.S. Civil Rights movement in the 1950s which had pretty much fully run its course by the mid-twenty-teens. In an interim period during this realignment but before it had fully run its course, the U.S. was basically a three party system with Northern Democrats (economically liberal, socially and militarily liberal), Southern Democrats (economically liberal, socially and militarily conservative), and Republicans (economically, socially, and militarily conservative), as the three de facto parties in terms of voting patterns in the 1980s. President Reagan tried to win over the working class, many of whom were Democrats driven by union membership (he was a union President himself) to the Republican coalition, but was largely unsuccessful in the long run; only when President Trump ran for office did this transition really take hold (and by then, the ranks of private sector blue collar union members was profoundly diminished).

There are 4 of the first 8 that are not arguable. If you include the dominant party period, you get 5. The language of the interview suggests that there were 4-5 realignments prior to the current one (below), so there would be a total of 5-6 realignments over 236 years governed by the current constitution.

  1. The transition from the pre-MAGA until the 2014 election to the post-MAGA political coalition in the Republican Party starting around 2015, in which Democrats and unaffiliated voter identification gained college educated voters, while the Republican party took non-college educated voters from the Democrats and unaffiliated voter identifications. The MAGA Republicans are a populist far-right party with authoritarian and Christian nationalist leanings. There are already plenty of Palestinian refugees in Arab countries, notably in Lebanon, Syria, Jordan - see Palestinian refugee camps:

Camps are set up by the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip to accommodate Palestinian refugees registered with UNRWA, who fled or were expelled during the 1948 Palestinian expulsion and flight after the 1948 Arab–Israeli War or in the aftermath of the Six-Day War in 1967, and their patrilineal descendants. UNRWA's mandate is to provide assistance to Palestinian refugees, including access to its refugee camps. For this purpose, it defines Palestinian refugees as "persons whose normal place of residence was Palestine during the period 1 June 1946 to 15 May 1948, and who lost both home and means of livelihood as a result of the 1948 conflict."

UNRWA also extends assistance to the patrilineal descendants of such refugees, as well as their legally adopted children.

The reasons for the unwillingness of the host countries to integrate these refugees are complex - e.g., in Jordan Palestinians with Jordanian citizenship (not refugees, but historical inhabitants of this area) constitute nearly the half of the population, while the ruling dynasty is representing another ethnic group (Hashemites) - the influx of the Palestinians thus represents a political threat to the King, as particularly came to surface in the events known as Black September (Jordanian Civil war) in 1970. I doubt that more removed countries, especially those in Europe or North America, have any particular preference to non-Palestinian refugees. Was there ever an effort to reduce the term of the elected members of the Federal Reserve?

The seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate. A full term is fourteen years. One term begins every two years, on February 1 of even-numbered years. A member who serves a full term may not be reappointed. A member who completes an unexpired portion of a term may be reappointed. All terms end on their statutory date regardless of the date on which the member is sworn into office.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/bios/board/default.htm

The fact that elected members can serve 14 years can lead to officials serving beyond the terms of an elected administration. Shorter terms might potentially increase accountability in the sense that Governors would be more directly responsive to the current administration and its economic priorities. This could lead to more immediate responsiveness to changing economic conditions and aligning policies with the goals of the elected government. Was there an effort to reduce the terms for the elected members of the Federal Reserve?
gold_answers:
The Commission on Money and Credit, established in 1957 and which published its report; Money and Credit: Their Influence on Jobs, Prices, and Growth in 1961, suggested that terms be reduced to 10 years:

The FRB should consist of five members, with overlapping ten-year terms, one expiring each odd-numbered year; members should be eligible for reappointment.

This would assure the President of one vacancy to be filled shortly after his inauguration while retaining the general stability of Board membership. The reduction in numbers should enhance the status of members, and the ten-year term combines a sufficient protection for independence, with some safeguard against superannuation.

Apart from the instruments of general monetary policy, the Board has important regulatory powers over member banks and some other financial institutions - for instance in the administration of the Bank Holding Company Act and of the anti-trust laws as applied to banks, in the approval or disapproval of applications for branches, mergers, and the like. These powers are vested in the Board, and the Board appears to treat them as non-delegable. Their exercise is exceedingly time-consuming and will become considerably more so if the Commission's recommendations in Chapter Six regarding the consolidation of functions of the Comptroller of the Currency and of the FDIC into the FRB are adopted. In this aspect of its work the Board has suffered from a malady that has plagued the other independent regulatory commissions, a congestion of detailed business at the top, to the detriment of the time and energy Board members can devote to the broad issues of monetary policy.

This recommendation was not taken up, perhaps for reasons given in a footnote of Power and Influence in the Federal Reserve System (Whittlesey 1963):

With terms starting February 1st as at present, this would enable the President to appoint a new Governor soon after taking office, whom he could then designate as Chairman. Such an arrangement would clearly open the way to political abuse and would make the issue of the Chairman's powers doubly significant. A similar result could be obtained with the present number of members and length of term of the Board simply by moving the terms forward or back so that they would expire in odd-numbered years.

This modification continued to be suggested though - the NYT carried an interview with a retiring member of the board, J. Charles Partlee, in 1986, in which he put the same suggestion forward:

I would also favor a reduction in the number of board members from seven to five.

Why would you do that?

The Fed has quite a large board, considering that the chairman has both the representational and executive-officer functions. Some years ago, we had only five sitting members and the board worked well at that size. Also, a member's term is a little too long in today's environment. I would not like to upset the general idea of terms staggered every two years, but if you had five members, that system would reduce the terms of each member from 14 to 10 years.

As far as I can tell from a quick search through proposed legislation, however, this proposal has not yet been put before Congress.

query:
Apportionment: Where is the actual language for "the method known as the method of equal proportions" in the U.S.C.?

In the United States Congress, there are two legislative bodies: the House of Representatives and the Senate. These two bodies are structured differently from the very beginning in Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution in that the Senate represents each U.S. state equally (two senators for each state) and House represents populations roughly equally: "Representatives ... shall be apportioned among the several States which may be included within this Union, according to their respective Numbers... The actual Enumeration shall be made ... within every subsequent Term of ten Years, in such Manner as they shall by Law direct."

So big states (w.r.t. population) get more representatives than do small states. The Constitution does not spell out how many total representatives there are in the House nor exactly the manner that the apportionment shall determine how many each state gets. It's just that every 10 years, we must have a Census for which the primary Constitutional purpose is to determine how the U.S. House of Representatives is apportioned among the now 50 U.S. states. The data from the Census gets used in a variety of ways and purposes, but this is the original primary purpose of the U.S. Decennial Census. It's a big deal.

(I would presume, in the European Union, that they have the same issue, but maybe settle the issue differently.)

So then, the specific number of U.S. representatives and the specific manner of proportionately distributing their seats to the various states is a matter of federal law (one notch lower than the Constitution) and is spelled out in U.S.C. Title 2. Well, not really completely spelled out, hence this question.

Okay, I know and understand what "the method known as the method of equal proportions" is. It's also known as the Huntington-Hill Method and is referred to as "the method known as the method of equal proportions" in §2a and §2b of U.S.C. Title 2.

There is also some useful history to read but I want to see the actual document in law that spells it out. Even if it was a report transmitted to Congress circa 1941, I would like to see what a federal judge would be saying that "this is what the law is" and I cannot find that.

Where is this "method of equal proportions" actually spelled out in the actual law? I cannot find it. I understand how the H-H method works and I have read a little history about it.
gold_answers:
There is nothing legally authoritative (e.g. codified regulations) beyond 2 U.S.C. §§ 2a and 2b, except for the legislative history of those acts.

In the case of Section 2a, this is the legislative history of 46 Stat. 26, c. 28, § 22 (June 18, 1929), 54 Stat. 162, c. 152 (Apr. 25, 1940), 55 Stat. 761, c. 470, § 1 (Nov. 15, 1941), and Pub.L. 104-186, Title II, § 201, 110 Stat. 1724 (Aug. 20, 1996).

In the case of Section 2b, this is the legislative history of 55 Stat. 762, c. 470, § 2(a) (Nov. 15, 1941).

But primarily, the relevant legislative history is the legislative history of the 1941 act mentioned above that introduced the concept.

Only one case has litigated § 2b and it does not address the mechanics of the equal proportions method. While many cases have been litigated under § 2a (59 annotations in some cases with more than one annotation from a single case), none of them addressed the meaning of the words "method of equal proportions". The census bureau, however, notes two cases that it looks to: Department of Commerce v. Montana, 112 S.Ct. 1415 (1992) and Franklin v. Massachusetts 112 S.Ct. 2767 (1992). The court in the first case found that the method adopted by Congress was constitutional and that its meaning was clarified by the National Academy of Science Committee report referenced by Congress in the legislative history involved in adopting the 1941 Act. The second case only touches on the issue tangentially because that issue was mooted by the resolution of the first case.

The meaning of the words "method of equal proportions" has never been reduced to a federal regulation.

The Congressionally intended meaning of the term method of equal proportions has always been sufficiently clear to avoid all disputes over it, even though it is not, for example, defined in Black's Law Dictionary.

The U.S. Census Bureau has, however, explained how the "method of equal proportions" works on multiple occasions in non-authoritative documents like press releases, and those together with secondary sources explaining it, could be offered up to prove it if necessary.

Things I do know about

  • I am aware that Lebanon has a dysfunctional political system with reserved positions by religion (Christian, Sunni, Shiite).

  • I am aware Hizbollah/Palestinians cause trouble. Israeli pressure, both directly on those groups, and on Lebanon to rein them in, can be problematic as well.

  • I am also aware that Syria's role in Lebanon is always toxic (already seen in song lyrics from 1982).

  • There was a political assassination some time ago that gets mentioned. But political assassinations are unfortunately not infrequent there.

But asides from Syria's civil war and its refugees, these are all longstanding issues. The Lebanon crisis seems to have been ongoing before Covid got started and while many countries got whacked by Covid, Lebanon does not seem to have been uniquely vulnerable to it.

So what caused this abysmal crisis in a country which, if anything, seemed to be in better shape right after their civil war than they are right now?

i.e. what's the really simple missing 5 minute intro and reminder to all those articles talking about Lebanese problems about how they got there? What's special about the last 5-6 years?
gold_answers:
In 2014-2017 the Middle East region saw multiple conflicts - some of them spilled over to Lebanon's territory. This hurt Lebanon's investment attractiveness - which was a big problem, because Lebanese pound was/is pegged to US dollar (at a rate of £L1,507.5 per US$1) since 1997, as a stabilizing measure after the severe devaluation of national currency after the civil war. Lebanese economics needed a constant influx of foreign capital to support this artificial exchange rate - mostly via tourism and financial sector; both of those were harmed by political instability in the region. Lebanese central bank was forced to engage in financial engineering, exchanging public debt it owned in national currency to foreign currency at a significant loss.

This is the point where crisis had started.

As a result, the liquidity crisis (in other words, the lack of US$ to exchange for Lebanese pounds) was averted in 2016, but Lebanese economy as a whole now had less money to circulate. And the regional instability was still far from gone, so the money leakage from Lebanese economy continued, and the central bank had to engage in course correction again and again.

By late 2018, Lebanese banks started imposing fees on operations their depositors made with foreign currency (currency those depositors owned!) to deter them from withdrawing USD in cash. At this point the general populace started becoming aware of the problems in the financial sector.

At this point, the crisis is already in full swing.

As multiple other public problems led to mass protests in 2019, commercial banks, fearing a bank run (very unsurprising in this situation), restricted access to depositors' funds. Unofficial exchange rates skyrocketed, and the following COVID pandemic only made things worse - by March 2021, the black market exchange rate was ~£L15,000 per US$1 - ten times the official rate from 2019. And the situation continues to deteriorate - as of today (February 2, 2023) black market rates are in excess of £L60k per US$1; the government is also finally acknowledges the devaluation officially by re-pegging the official rate at £L15k per US$1.

P.S. You really could say that Lebanon was better off right after the civil war than today. The "other problems" I mentioned in the last paragraph included the lack of stable electricity and water supply, rampant pollution, and even more rampant corruption. The financial crisis was really only one more sign of Lebanese government failing to solve problems the population faced after the civil war.
